utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, I notice that Mr. Pavkovic is not here, and this may be something that has happened at the last minute I gather.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've only known about it for about four or five minutes, Your Honour. Apparently it has something to do with a medical situation. That's all I can tell you. I have no communication with him that he's waiving his appearance. We're trying to get that done right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's no reason to think that the evidence which is likely to be led today will be of particular significance to his criminal responsibility, I imagine, and I doubt if there's any reason why we shouldn't just carry on. Obviously, if there was an issue arising out of it you would have the opportunity to raise the matter and re-call a witness if that were to prove necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that may be true with regard to the first witness; I'm not sure it is with regard to the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, by the second you may have more information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think that's no doubt the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I take it you're content we carry on for the moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You're Honour, I can't represent that he is waiving his appearance, so I am not content that we carry on, but if that's Your Honour's wish, you go right ahead. I'm not agreeing to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, you don't state any specific objection. I note also that you don't consent to the proceedings in his absence and we'll consider the position briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you want to say something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we -- we have actually been in communication with someone named Maja at the detention centre who says that he's going for some kind of an examination and that she will send -- she will secure and send a waiver. When that happens, I don't know, but that's the latest information we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, are you wanting time to make that arrangement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I think it's -- I think it has not changed anything, except I'm giving you some more information. It hasn't changed my position, but I think there'll be a waiver forthcoming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Mr. Ackerman. We are satisfied that it's appropriate for us to proceed to hear the evidence of the next witness. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The next witness will be Reshit Salihi. And, Your Honour, we'll need your assistance in administering the oath to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And paragraphs, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is going to give evidence regarding events in Celine village, Orahovac municipality, regarding paragraphs 25 through 32, 72(a) and 77 (a) and (d). He is a 92 bis (D) witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that becomes now 92 ter, I think, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The way that rule reads, you probably have to have -- or you do have to have him verify the accuracy of his transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's correct, and we've had some discussion about that now in our office. Now, how we deal with that when there is not a -- there -- this witness does not read. There is not a transcript in his language, and there is an audio tape or a video-tape but he has not had a chance to review that. I think that I will just simply confirm with him that he gave true and accurate testimony at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think that's all I would expect of you. Can we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for him to come in, Your Honour, I would indicate that the transcript is Exhibit 2337, that was his testimony on the 19th and 22nd of April, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And his written statement was incorporated in that testimony. The written statement including a supplement was -- is our Exhibit 2336. It's referred to in the Slobodan Milosevic transcript as Exhibit 104 and is referred to at page 3545.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Salihi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the following words after me: I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That I will speak the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've previously testified in this Tribunal in the Slobodan Milosevic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And our records indicate that that was on the 19th and 22nd of April, 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March. This all happened on the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, sir. I was referring to the date that you came here to the Tribunal and testified in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I can't remember the date when I came here. I'm not educated; I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's quite all right, sir. You recall testifying in that case, and at that time did the -- did the testimony you give, was that your true and accurate evidence about the events as you could remember them at that time?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, everything was true because I lived those things, I experienced them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in addition, part of your evidence in that trial included your written statement to the ICTY, a written statement of 29 April 1999, and a supplement of the 30th of January, 2002. When you came here this week to testify in this trial, was -- were those prior statements read back to you?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you satisfied and can you tell this Court that your evidence in those statements is true and accurate to the best of your information and belief?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Everything is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would tender Exhibits 2336, the statements, and 2337, the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Salihi, I understand you were born and raised in the village of Celine in Rahovec municipality?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're a farmer, you're the son of a farmer, and the grandson of a farmer?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your evidence, sir, you described an attack that occurred on your village on the 25th of March, 1999. How big --

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How big was your village, about how many people?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: There are about 250 houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And do you know approximately how many people lived in those houses?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I could say over 2.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in your statement of April 1999, in the English version at page 2, paragraph 2; in the B/C/S, page 2, also paragraph 2, you say that: About 3.00 that afternoon you saw a large number of Serb policemen arriving. And you describe them as wearing --

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You describe them as wearing black uniforms. Could you tell us how you --

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- able to identify them as policemen, rather than, say, VJ soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object. That's kind of leading, and I object to it, the "rather than VJ soldiers," part. There's no indication of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Usually a leading question is one where the examiner suggests the answer. Using that test, I doubt if it is leading, Mr. Ackerman, but I think there's a point there. Could we just be a bit more open in the question, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think because there are three categories that we're all aware of here, three general categories regularly referred to by people; to confine the question to two, I think, could have been arguably seen as inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I could either expand it or reduce it, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think reducing it is probably better.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you tell us how you were able to determine that they were policemen?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Because we knew. We knew that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did you know?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Well, I knew because I saw them when they entered the village, and I knew that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 2 of the English at paragraph 4; in B/C/S, it's page 3, paragraph 2, you mention that after you had been in the forest for three days, the next morning a group of about 40 policemen in blue camouflage uniforms with white armbands came to the forest area where you were. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your 1999 statement you -- you described them as wearing blue berets, but you later on corrected that. Can you tell us now what your best recollection is of what kind of head wear they were wearing.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: The policemen you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They had all the colours, they changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say that they fired their weapons in the air and got all the people to come out. There were some 10.000 or so people.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The men --

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, because there were many refugees there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say at that time the men were separated from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were these policemen saying anything to you while this was going on?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: When they separated us, they lined us up. First of all, they asked for money. Whatever we had in foreign currency they took away from us and they wouldn't take any Serbian money.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they say anything else to you during this process?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They were speaking amongst themselves, and we understood a little bit. And they said if we won't have enough, then we'll use our knives and cut them up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, do you -- do you understand Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand it fairly well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 4 of the English, paragraph 5; page 5 of the B/C/S, paragraph 3, at the time you made your statement in 1999 you didn't -- you were not certain about the fate of your brother Faik and his family or of the Zeqiri family, although you say while you were in Albania you had seen a newspaper article, indicating that they were dead. Since then, have you found out what happened to Faik and his family and the Zeqiri family?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it very well when it happened. First of all, Bajram, my eldest brother, was killed. Then the infantry came and they killed all of them on the 25th of March at 4.00 p.m., and I knew about it. But when I went to the forest I did not tell them. I told them only about Bajram. I told them Bajram was killed, but about the other ones, I told them later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did you -- did you see that happen? I know you saw your brother Bajram killed; you told us that before.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was before my eyes that it happened. This is where the bullet pierced him and he fell down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But as far as Faik and his family and the Zeqiri family, I understood you heard shooting and you heard screams, but at the time you did not actually see what happened to them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I couldn't come out and see how they were being killed, but hear everything because I was close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you return to Kosovo after you had been deported, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Home?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: From Albania?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Three months later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you discover anything about Faik and his family at that time?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, they were killed, and when the foreigners came and they took their notes, everything they had to note down, and then we buried them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you discover their bodies when you returned then three months later?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did you find them?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: The same place they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The last place you had seen them?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there a mosque in Celine?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was it intact and undamaged on the 25th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: It was hit. The mosque was destroyed when they came in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see it at the time it was destroyed or only after you returned?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No, it was after I came from Albania that I saw it because I couldn't see it then. I was leaving. But when we returned, we saw that the whole village had been burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you,

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no more questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order will be: General Lazarevic, General Pavkovic, General Ojdanic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Salihi. My name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for General Vladimir Lazarevic, and I will have a few brief questions for you. In your statement you described that on the 25th of March in the morning the VJ -- some VJ units appeared around the village. That was at 5.00 a.m., as far as I could see from your statement; therefore, I hope you will agree with me that at that time it was still dark in the village?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: When we got up in the morning, when I woke up, we were surrounded and we saw it was the army. They surrounded us, but they did not damage the civilian --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I only wanted to know whether it was dark.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was morning. It was morning, but it was not dark. It was light.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to tell us that by the end of March it already gets lighter at 5.00 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you how it was like the morning I woke up. I think it was light, and the army had surrounded the village. I don't know what you're trying to do with this, whether it was dark or light; I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm just trying to clarify some things, and I need your assistance as regards that. On the 27th of September, a few days ago that is, you had an interview with our learned friends from the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And everything you stated then is absolutely correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, everything is correct. I experienced all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no more questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman -- or, Mr. Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Salihi. My name is Aleksander Aleksic, attorney-at-law, and together with my colleague Mr. John Ackerman, I appear on behalf of Nebojsa Pavkovic. I have three brief questions for you, and could you keep your answers brief, only a yes or no. You described the events in detail. You did not have any contact with the soldiers there, you yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The NATO bombing began on the 24th of March. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Up until then, things were peaceful in your village and there had been no incidents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was no incident before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Aleksic. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With the background of late yesterday afternoon in mind, I'm pleased to advise the Trial Chamber that I have conferred with my colleague Mr. Visnjic, and we indeed have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I can confirm, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I consulted Mr. Visnjic as well; I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, as usual I do have some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Salihi. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. Ivetic and Mr. Ogrizovic I appear on behalf of Mr. Lukic before this Tribunal. I wanted to go back to one part of your testimony today when my learned friend Mr. Hannis attempted to clarify how you saw uniforms. When he asked you how did you know that these men were policemen you said: I saw them enter the village. My question is the following: Did you personally know any of the people who entered the village?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: We didn't know them personally, but we knew that they were policemen. How could we talk to them? But I know that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 8, line 7 you say in your answer: They had all the different colours they changed. Does this mean that irrespective of the colour of uniforms, all uniformed men to you are policemen?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No, the policemen were clear to us. We knew that they were policemen, but they were split up in groups. And they had different uniforms, but they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any insignia on those uniforms?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They had red ribbons on the right arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And anything on the uniform itself?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I couldn't -- we couldn't look at them very attentively. You know, we couldn't raise our eyes up to them; we didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Were these uniforms black, as you've told us, or were they of any other colours?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They had black uniforms, but they had also other colours. They kept changing. We saw different colours every ten minutes. To me, it doesn't make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. I would like to go back briefly to the point in time when you saw the armed men approaching you. As I was reading your statements, I wasn't clear whether you had stayed at your farm or whether you had hid in a house that was close to your farm or whether you had gone to the forest. What of the three things happened?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Look here, when it became dark, then I went to the forest. But until then I didn't dare leave my house because they might have killed me. They were very close to where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, you were in your house?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Not inside the house, but outside because we didn't dare stay inside for fear that they might set the house on fire, because this is what they usually did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you do before the noon while these troops were approaching you?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing. We just stayed and waited, fearing that they might come and do to us the worst, as they usually did to other people. They killed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The farm that you were at, was it surrounded by a wall?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us how high the wall was.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: About 2 metres high.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say that Bajram got up, he stood up and then he was hit. What was the position of your brother, Bajram, before he was hit?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: He got up to see what was happening, and there was a house about 30 metres away from us and the policemen were there. When Bajram got up to see, just to see what was going on, they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that moment, was Bajram standing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: When he was killed, of course he fell on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before he was hit, was he standing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: All of us were standing on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How is it possible for somebody standing on the ground to be hit in the stomach if at that time he was hiding behind a 2-metre-high wall?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: When Bajram was killed, my brother, he was outside the wall. You must understand me well. He was outside a wall at the corner of the wall, and they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you also outside of the wall?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the others who were with you, were they also outside of the wall?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Those who were killed were outside the wall. I myself was inside the wall. The difference between us was just 1 metre; the wall divided us.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, distance between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see when your brother Bajram was hit, did you see that happen?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: He was about 2 metres far from me, of course I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Wasn't there a 2-metre-high wall between the two of you then, and you were on one side of the wall and then there is the 2-metre-high wall and he is on the other side of that wall. And you could see him stand up and you could see him being hit; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Look here, don't provoke me here. I told you he was just a metre away from the wall. When he stood up, they hit him and killed him. Don't tell me 1 metre, 2 metres, please don't provoke me because I came here to tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am asking you because I want to hear the truth from you. Can you please explain, we have just heard from you that you were within the courtyard, that your brother was outside of the courtyard, on the other side of that wall. And you've also told us that that wall was 2 metres high. Can you now explain how you happened to -- saw your brother being hit?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: We were, both of us, on the same side of the wall, but he went out to see the corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I really don't understand what you have just told us.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I, too, am not understanding it. I didn't come here to tell lies. You know that my brother was killed, and I think you are provoking me, this side or that side, I am telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm not provoking you; I'm just looking for an explanation. Were you on the same side of the wall together with your brother?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I told you, we were on the same side. I was there. He just got up at the corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Salihi, it is clear to all of us that you're saying you were very close to your brother at the time he was killed. The particular point that Mr. Lukic is trying to be clear about is whether you could actually see him at the very moment he was killed or whether the wall at that point obstructed your view of your brother, albeit you knew that he had been shot. Now, could you actually see him at the moment he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw him when they killed him. I was 1 metre away. I saw it very well. I saw him firing a burst of fire, and he fell immediately down. I was at the corner of the wall, and then I saw him falling down. And then I went -- withdrew a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Salihi. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It others who had joined you that morning, where were they?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They know then we moved away because we -- the infantry troops approached. So we fled wherever we could. We didn't know where we were going. I personally went to the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say around 3.00 that afternoon, we saw a great number of Serb policemen arriving and approaching my farm. We had been joined by Miftare Zeqiri and 14 members of his family at our farm. You're talking about your family farm. What about the other people who had joined you, where were they? On which side of the wall were they?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: The dead, the people who got killed? You mean the group of Miftare Zeqiri, this is what you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about the moment when they joined you at your farm and when your brother was killed.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: We just wanted to leave from there. We didn't -- we didn't dare stay at home because they set the houses on fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This -- this question, Mr. Salihi, is to find out where Faik and his family and the Zeqiri family were when a number were killed. Were they inside in your compound when they were killed or were they outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Zeqir's family and the brother and the children, they were outside, outside -- in the courtyard, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. If they were in the courtyard, were they outside of the wall or within the wall? I'm not sure that we have received a good interpretation.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I think the interpretation is good. I told you, they were outside the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. All of you were then sitting outside of the wall at the moment when the Serb forces were approaching you. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No. All of them were outside, but I was at the corner of the wall with my brother, as I already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I just don't see a possibility to clarify this fully. I'll move on. When you are talking about the men approaching you, you say that they wore dark grey bandannas on their heads. How were these bandannas tied? Could you please tell us?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you because I didn't go up to them to see how their bandannas were tied, as you are asking me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is a bandanna tied around one's head a customary part of a police uniform?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: It's not customary, but this is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is a normal police uniform usually black?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I told you, they had worn all sorts of colours, but we didn't dare go close to them because they might have killed us, as they did kill many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could we agree that black is not a customary police uniform colour. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that the witness said "they know it," not "I know it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, before all of this happened, before the 24th of March when you say things were quiet, did you from time to time see police officers or policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They came there, they went, but we were not paying any attention to them. That didn't interest us. We defended our own affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you remember what colour the normal police uniform in Celine was at the time before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tell you, sir, that before the war they came very rarely, if to say not at all to Celine before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before the war when you saw a policeman, can you remember what colour of uniform he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. They had black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the incident when Agim Ramadani was killed?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, when they forced us to leave the mountain in the morning of the 28th, they divided men from women. And at that moment, Agim Ramadani --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can see all this in your statement. Let me ask you this: How many people were there in the same place where you were?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I cannot tell you the exact number, but I do know that there were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Where were you among all those people?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I was with them. We were all together when they divided us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in the middle, at any of the ends?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: In the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say in one of your statements that there were around 10.000 people there?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: In my statement I said 4 or 5.000, not 10.000, but you must understand it that there were a lot of people. It might be true that they were 10.000. Who counted them?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And you are telling us that you saw this young man being killed in a crowd of some 5.000 people?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: They always asked the young men to come out of the group. They maltreated them. They even maltreated me. They beat us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next thing you say in the Albanian page 5, paragraph 2; the English version, page 4, paragraph 3; and the B/C/S version, page 4, paragraph 4, you are describing a group of policemen in blue camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: This is true, because there were many policemen. They changed every 10, 20 metres, you know, there were so many policemen, but we didn't dare look at them carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would that colour be closer to the colour of uniforms that you had seen before the war on police officers, or do you still claim that you saw policemen wearing black uniforms before the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, one question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not a fair question to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Mr. Salihi. I'll ask you one question at a time. On that particular occasion you saw policemen in blue camouflage uniforms. Could you please point to that colour, the blue colour, here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I told you once and I'm telling you now, they had different colours. I can't remember now all these colours. I told you we didn't raise our head and look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is your description, your statement, you said that you had seen blue camouflage uniforms; that's why I'm asking you whether you see the same blue colour here in the courtroom, colour blue. You can, you may, raise your head and you can look around yourself.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Their clothes were black, but they had also what we call green grass colour. It was mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, this part of your statement where you say that the policemen, the second group of policemen, wore blue camouflage uniforms has not been recorded correctly. Is that what you're saying today?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I told you that they had different colours, but I cannot explain to you which group wore which colour because they kept changing, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I've asked you and I've given you a possibility and I give you another possibility to point something of blue colour here in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, there, the flag, that colour, and black.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May the record indicate he's indicated the UN flag behind Judge Chowhan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will now, Mr. Hannis, but what's not clear to me is what the reference to black was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I thought he said "with black." [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did policemen before the war wear black camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not camouflage, black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only black uniforms, not camouflage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the answer --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the group wearing blue camouflage uniforms, you saw men wearing red berets on their heads. The group with blue camouflage uniforms also wore red berets - is that correct - were they also policemen?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that in the afternoon a number of trucks arrived and that you were ordered to get on those trucks. Can you please tell us how many trucks arrived.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I don't know how many. I did not count them. They were in line in a convoy. We were told to board the trucks, and we didn't know where they were sending us. But we learned that later that we were going towards Zhur, towards Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you all manage to get on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Everybody got on the trucks. The people who were there got on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're telling us that 10.000 people managed to get on those trucks?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I didn't say "10.000." 4 or 5.000, because there were women as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that some 4 to 5.000 people got on those trucks after all?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's been asked and answered. He's already said everybody got on the trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand your fixation with this detail, Mr. Lukic. You know, you expect this man to be able to assess accurately a large crowd. It's just unrealistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, that's what we are trying to prove, that he was not able and is not able --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, common sense tells you that. Whether there was a large question is the real question, not whether there was 10.000 or 4 to 6.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you. [Interpretation] Could we have Exhibit D -- 6D78 displayed on e-court. This exhibit was downloaded from the EDS. We have a draft translation of this document into English. Could we have the English version displayed on the screen, the draft translation of the original document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While this is being done, I'm going to ask you, Mr. Salihi --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I inquire of my colleague whether this is a full translation or a partial translation? The English doesn't seem to be as lengthy as the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is partial. We always do that when we use only Serbian document that we do not have translated. So this is a draft and unofficial translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihi, you told us that there was no KLA presence in your village.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: There wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a document here that we received from the Prosecution. It's the minutes of Shehu Agram's [phoen] statement, who otherwise was a KLA member. On page 1 we see the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see page 2 now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is if he knows that there was KLA in his village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you know the answer to that, so it must be a different question you want to put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe he can reconcile his memory when he sees it or maybe he knows this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he can't see it, for a start. And really, it is very difficult to see how this is going to assist. If you have a question, put the question. It doesn't depend on putting the detail of this statement. You can take from this the question that you want to put. This is a foundation for your question. But you're certainly going to cause confusion here if you go into detail, unless this is a person he particularly knows. If you want to establish he knows him, that might be different, but if he's simply a third party as far as he's concerned, then going into the detail of his statement takes us nowhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Salihi, you stated yourself that it was at a long time that you had not seen a Serbian policeman or a Serbian soldier before the 25th of March, 1999. Would you agree with me if I said that the reason for this being that the area around your village and including your village was under KLA control, at least a few months before the NATO campaign began.

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I don't agree. No, I don't agree because there was no KLA in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a KLA presence in the forests and hills around Celine?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: I didn't keep watch on them, where they stayed, what their bases were, where their bases were, I didn't pay attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that in Celine, close to the mosque, there was a KLA position in the centre of village?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: In Celine there wasn't any present -- presence. I was born there and I grew up there and I don't understand what you're saying, the things that you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person by the name of Agron Shehu [phoen]? Truth be told me is from Mala Krusha?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No. No, I don't know him. I've given my statement about my own village, Celine. I don't know about other villages. I've given my statement about the massacre in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I accept your explanation concerning this Agron person. Is it correct that the KLA organised the civilian life as well, in particular the 124th KLA Brigade organised civilian administration, civilian authorities in the villages of Velika Krusa, Celine, Nogovac, Mala Hoca, and Brestovac. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no foundation for that question --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, when I put the document on the screen you tell me don't put the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have the document regarding this question as well, it's 6D77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no doubt you do. But the point I'm making to you is you have no foundation for thinking that this witness will have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's made his position abundantly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He just told us: I lived there the whole life. He must have known at that time that even the civilian life was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, once you establish a basis for this question, then we may permit it; and that will mean, first of all, exploring his knowledge of the activity of the KLA in the area, which, as I understand it, he said he paid absolutely no attention to. Now, whether that's a realistic position for him to take is a matter on which you, no doubt, will make submissions, but you've got the answer to the question, I think, already. It's predictable what's coming. And there must -- you will have to bear -- bring some sort of sense of proportion to the way in which you're cross-examining about the KLA. You cannot, a la Milosevic, constantly put propositions to witness about the KLA when you know that they have very little or claim to have very little knowledge of these activities. We haven't got endless time for this purpose. You will have ample opportunity to present the case of your own. I know that in theory you're entitled to cross-examine on all of these, but we have to bring a sense of proportion to the whole proceedings. We're spending all this time making no progress whatsoever when you've got loads of evidence obviously tucked away there to use in due course. And if you use all your time here in sort of cross-examination, it will be very difficult for the Court to allow you an equivalent amount of time to lead the positive evidence you claim to have.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, this was my last question, so I didn't intend to have too many questions like late Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have an amazingly bad habit of intervening at the wrong time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So taking in mind -- having in mind your guidances, this was our last question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Salihi, I have no more questions for you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, I just want to go back and clear up something regarding when your brother Bajram was killed, at page 18, line 12 of today's transcript, and I need to ask you: Did Bajram have a weapon at the time he was killed?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Never. Bajram never had a gun in his hand, and he was not a soldier at the time. He never completed military service for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Because the transcript was translated -- your answer was translated as: I saw him when they killed him. I was 1 metre away. I saw him firing a burst of fire and he fell immediately down. So I take it from your answer that's not correct. He wasn't firing a weapon because he didn't have one?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No. Bajram did not have a weapon. He was killed in front of me, right before my eyes. They killed even little children, one-month-old babies. So many people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand your previous answers, was he looking around a corner of the wall when he was shot?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He went a little outside the wall at the corner to be able to see what was going on. Because there were policemen at another house. We didn't know where these policemen were, but they shot at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And whether you were inside the wall or outside the wall, was there anything between you and him obstructing your view of him when he got shot?

utterances.speaker: RESHIT SALIHI
utterances.text: No. There was nothing between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Salihi, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give that evidence. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much for having me here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, our next witness is Agim Jemini.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same area?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. He is also from Celine village and Orahovac municipality. His testimony relates to paragraphs 25 through 32, 72(a), 77(a) and (d). And he's a 92 bis (D) witness as well -- or 92 ter I should say, Your Honour. It will take me a while to get used to the new number. His transcript from his testimony of 7 June, 2002, it's our Exhibit number 2353 and it incorporates his statement of 17 July 1999 and a 3 June 2002 addendum, which in the Milosevic transcript were numbered Exhibit 270 and it is our Exhibit Number 2338.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's -- there are photographs referred to in the transcript of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Milosevic. Are they to --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Those two photographs were given one number, number 260 in Milosevic at page 6537 in the transcript. And those photos are our Exhibit Numbers P2339 and 2340.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jemini.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jemini. I want to establish a background for some of your written evidence that we've proposed to submit to the Court. You previously testified here at this Tribunal in the Slobodan Milosevic case on the 7th of June, 2002. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, sir, is the testimony you gave at that time true and accurate to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time a written statement of 17 July 1999 and a 3 June 2002 addendum that you had made to ICTY OTP investigators was incorporated in your evidence. Did you have a chance to go over that statement and that addendum prior to today?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you satisfied that they are accurate and correct and you would confirm that to this Court at this time?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I said the transcript is Exhibit P2353. The statement and the addendum are 2330 -- sorry, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 2338 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: 2338, yes, thank you. And I would tender those at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, I understand you were born in 1960 in Celine, in Rahovec municipality, in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're married with four children?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could you tell us when you did your mandatory military service?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was your job or specialty?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I was administrator to the battalion command in Skopje or it's also called cata [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I understand from your written evidence that you were the mayor for many years in Celine. Can you tell us how long you were mayor?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: From 1988 to today, so maybe it is 16 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in 1999 how big was Celine village, approximately how many houses and how many people?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: In 1999 there were approximately 2.000 inhabitants in Celine and 253 households.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the ethnicity of the people who lived in the village?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: All of them Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence, in your written statement, and your testimony you talked about an attack on your village that occurred on the 25th of March, 1999. Can you tell us, what were the forces that came to Celine on that date?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. On the 25th of March, 1999, at about 5.30 in the morning the village was surrounded by APCs and tanks of the Serb military forces. And from that moment they started shooting, shelling, burning, killing, and all the other things that happened in Celine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You -- you've told us in some detail about that in your written statement. But I have a question about the particular forces, can you tell us whether they were military, police, or something else.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What kind of uniforms were they wearing?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The uniform was blue camouflage with patterns, with different colours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. On their left upper arm was the eagle of the Serbian army, the two-headed eagle, the normal eagle that the Serbian army held. And they had various ribbons in various places.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you describe in your statement in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, Your Honour, this might be a good point to break. I won't be done in two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I understand that. And certainly the -- so far the answers are not consistent with the written statement, unless there's a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Jemini, we need to break now for half an hour. So could you please leave the courtroom. You'll return at 11.00. Meanwhile, you'll be shown where to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And we will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, your evidence will now continue. Mr. Hannis will continue to examine you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, just before we broke I'd asked you about what kind of uniforms these military forces were wearing when they came to your village on the 25th. Your answer as translated was: "Blue camouflage with patterns with different colours." I note in your written statement from July of 1999, page 2, paragraph 4 in all three versions, that you indicated they were all wearing green/brown camouflage uniforms. Can you tell us which it was or why there's a difference between what you said today and what you said in your written statement.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't think there is any difference. Maybe it was misinterpreted, but the uniforms they were wearing were brown-green, as I have stated in my statements, camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that they had with them vehicles, APCs and tanks. Do you recall approximately how many tanks there were?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The village was surrounded on all sides by tanks and APCs, and I would say that on every side there were at least two or three tanks. So a total of 12 tanks altogether, including APCs, armoured cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In your statement, English page 2, paragraph 4; page 2, paragraph 3 of the B/C/S; page 3, the last paragraph of the Albanian, you describe where the men that you presumed were the commanders of these forces, where they were during the day in a house next to where you were hiding. I'd like to show you first of all a photograph that's been marked as Exhibit P2339, which from your prior testimony we understand is a picture from the place where you and your cousin were hiding that day. It will come up on your screen in a moment, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can rotate it 90 degrees to the left or 270 to the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And from where was that taken?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It was taken from the place of the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Can we enlarge that one step up? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on that photograph can you see where you saw the men you described as commanders, where they were located? And if the usher could help you, we have a pen with which you could mark on the screen, and I'd you actually to use that pen and mark with an X the location where you saw the commanders.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The commanders were in the house opposite to where I was, about 10, 12 metres away, and it was in the balcony number 1 here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on what floor of that building is that balcony located? Is that the ground floor, the next floor up, the third floor?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: On the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And approximately what was the distance from where they were standing to where you were looking from?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: In the picture, you can see it is very close, 10 to 12 metres away I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC58, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And next I'd like to show you Exhibit 2340, and I'll have you make a mark on this one as well. And I understand from your evidence before that you were on the top floor of the building where you and your cousin were hiding. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, do you see another photograph on your screen at the moment?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were -- you and your cousin were hiding.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you use that pen again and mark on there where you and he were?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: This is the place we were hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot of that one and give it the next IC number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before doing that, does that photograph help us at all, does it show where the commanders were -- of the building in which the commanders were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll let the witness answer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you understand the question. In this photograph can you see the building with the balcony where the commanders were standing?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: For the moment I cannot see -- in this picture, I cannot see it. We need another picture for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC59, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if we could show Exhibit P2356 to the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to show you one more photo, Mr. Jemini. You describe in your statement how well you were hiding. You saw your parents and other relatives taken to a spot and shot. Can you tell us what this is a photograph of now?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: This is a photograph of the house we lived in and where I was hiding, and there was a distance of 80 metres between the two houses. In the house across where I was, the family members were brought out of the basement, my mother, father, my uncle, his wife, and his son, and they were forced to leave the basement and were placed in front of this house, here in this place. And they asked them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do have that information, Mr. Jemini. We're just trying to identify the places. Now, Mr. Hannis is going to ask you to mark certain things on this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We do have your evidence from your prior testimony and your written statement. So could you mark on this photograph if it shows the spot where your relatives were shot.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Here, in this place, where they were shot, whereas these other sides, these two X's, indicate where they were asked to give money.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I understand the two X's on the left side of the screen is where they were first asked for money and now --

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: When they had that conversation and when they were maltreated, one X shows the spot where they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we give that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do, it would help me, Mr. Hannis, if we could also mark the building that has the basement and the building where the witness was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll ask a question about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: From where was this photograph taken, from which spot?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It was taken from the place I was hiding, across on the top floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So the house that you were hiding in does not appear in this photograph; correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No, it does not appear because I took the photograph from the window of the place I was hiding in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I understand now entirely, Mr. Hannis, and it follows that the building --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- at the X is the building where the basement is, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what the reference to the basement is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's where the family were hiding before they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Yes, I'm sorry, I'm getting basement and attic confused, Your Honour. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the building where the commanders were talking on the radio does not appear in this photograph either, does it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Not here, but you could see it in the other photo where the balcony was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we give this the next IC number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC60, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jemini, I want to go to page 5, paragraph 3 of the English; page 5, paragraph 1 of the B/C/S; and it is page 6, paragraph 4 of the Albanian. You describe how you and your cousin fled that house where you had been hiding and went to Zrze. And on the way you passed a "murder scene near Bellacerka, a river bed near the railway line." Can you tell us approximately how many bodies you saw at that murder scene?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It was 3.30 in the morning when we passed by the murder scene. The number was around 40. I am not precise. That is the -- roughly the number of the massacred people from Bellacerka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And anything you can tell us about the clothing they were wearing and whether or not they had any visible injuries or wounds?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The bodies you saw there, can you tell us how they were dressed and whether or not they had any visible wounds?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. They were all killed. They were in civilian clothes, and they were people from Bellacerka.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you see any injuries on their bodies?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: At that moment we were so upset and shocked at what we saw, so the only thing we saw was they were dead, full of injuries, but we didn't look further than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we next show the witness a page from the Kosovo atlas, Exhibit P615, at page 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, we'll put a map up on your screen, and when it's there I would like you to use the pen again and mark on it for us three different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And could we -- near the centre of the map, could we blow it up a couple of notches? Maybe one more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you able to see your village on this map?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could you draw a circle around Celine and put a -- put the number 1 in the circle?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's fine. And then can you show us the approximate location of where you saw the bodies in the river bed and put the number two in a circle at that location.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. Here, it's here. That's the point where the railway and the river cross. It's a bridge or there is also irrigation canal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And then I see on the map Zrze is the village where you and your cousin went; correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we take a screen shot and give that the next IC number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC61, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, I'm sorry to rush through this but we have limited time. I want to ask you about whether there was a mosque in Celine in 1999?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it damaged during March of 1999 when the offensive against your village took place?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Because we were hiding during the day in the periphery of the village, and we could hear the explosion that destroyed the mosque totally. And when we went there in the evening, we could see that it was totally destroyed. We could hear where we were in the outskirts, about 1 kilometre from it, the sound of the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show Exhibit P1800 to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have one last photograph I'd like you to take a look at, sir, and tell us if you can recognise what is depicted there. Can you tell the Judges what that is?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. This is a photo of the totally destroyed mosque. This is rubble from the mosque. This is part of the minaret where the round is here. As you can see it the minaret is almost totally destroyed and there is a part that is still intact here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that how it looked for the first time after you heard that loud explosion?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jemini. I have no more questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order is: General Pavkovic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Milutinovic, General Ojdanic, General Lukic, and General Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jemini. I have several questions for you, and if you'll listen very carefully to my questions and try to answer them as briefly as possible we can get through this much more quickly. I want to begin by referring to your statement, paragraph 2, you talk about the offensive that began on the 25th of March and you said this: "The whole population of the village was still present because we had no KLA presence and there was no reason for anyone to leave." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if there had been a KLA presence there, then I presume the converse of what you said would be that there would have been a reason for people to leave because of the KLA presence; correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. Your statement was that: "We had no KLA presence, so there was no reason to leave." If there had been a KLA presence, then I take it there would have been a reason to leave?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. If we had a KLA presence, we would have a reason to defend ourselves. But without its presence there, there was no reason for the entry of the military forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you tell us that there was no reason for anyone to leave your village because there was no KLA, then if there had been KLA wouldn't that have been a reason for you to leave the village? Isn't that the logical conclusion to draw from your statement?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It would be a logical conclusion if there was KLA presence because the Serbian forces wanted to drive the KLA out of its positions. And in those cases, the population had to leave because of the offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, yes, exactly. And that's -- that's why you felt safe. If the KLA had been there, you knew that your village then would have drawn the attention of the Serb forces, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, you pretty much said that in Milosevic trial at page 6549 when you said: "Everywhere the Serbian army and police entered into areas where there was KLA." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: But in our case, that was not so because they entered a village where there was no presence of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well -- and of course you don't know whether they believed KLA was there or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I knew what was going on in the village because I was the mayor and I was living there. That is why I am saying I was sure that there was no KLA presence and we didn't expect the Serbian forces to enter the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know, but I think you misunderstood my question. My question was: You don't have any way of knowing if the Serbian forces believed that KLA was in your village, do you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: There was no way how we could know what they thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Before the 25th of March, everything was peaceful in your village, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And it was only after NATO began its attacks that the war came to your village; true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
