utterances.text: And you talk about the forces that were surrounding your village and shelling it, and what you say in your statement at paragraph 3 is that: "It did not appear that they were aiming at the people. It seemed they were trying to scare everyone in the village." That's true, too?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if the forces believed that the KLA was hiding in your village, that might be a way to get the KLA to expose themselves, to flee the village, or to clear the village of civilians so they could attack the KLA. That also makes sense, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you talked to us about these commanders who you -- whose radio transmission you claim to have heard. You said they had hand-held radios?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that you not only could hear what they were saying, but you could hear what was coming to them through these radios. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look, please, at -- at IC58.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If we could have that put up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, just so that -- just so that we're all clear, this is taken from that window that you claim to have been observing things from, and where you've marked that little red X, that is the place where you say these commanders were standing. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So that's a place that you say was 10 or 12 metres away from where you were; correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So now I'd like you to now look at IC59, please. And that picture shows with a red X the spot where you were observing these events and from where you claim to have seen and heard these commanders, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that building which was directly out in front of your window where you were looking out, according to the last picture, is not visible in this picture, is it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No, it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we can see a great deal more than 10 or 12 metres out in front of that building where you claim to have been watching, can't we?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: This is the house from where my parents were taken, and it's about 80 to 100 metres away from where I was staying. It was the place where my family was living, while the house that I described that is 10 to 12 metres away is behind this tree here and you cannot see it, unfortunately. So that's the fifth house in the row.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let's blow the picture up at that spot where that tree is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we do that? Can we zoom in on it there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We're going to try to do that. Not that tree. Not that tree. The tree in -- the tree to the right of the white structure, right there. Blow it up some more, and some more, and some more. Now, you claim that the house is behind that tree?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It's -- yeah, it's right here, 12 metres -- it was the other photograph that was clearer that you can see that distance, 10 to 12 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, are you saying that house is to the left of that little tree there that we see in the middle?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's a great deal more than 10 or 12 metres from where you were, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't think it's more than 12 metres. I can't tell you exactly the distance, but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you heard these commanders -- I want to go back now to IC59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is IC59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is. IC --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to IC58.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the place where you've marked the X, they were actually standing out on that balcony or were they inside the house where the balcony is?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: On the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So they were standing right there on that unfinished balcony; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the -- this place you were observing from is this window this picture is taken from. With them standing out there on that balcony, you certainly couldn't just stand up in that window and look around, could you, because they'd have seen you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you claim that these commanders that were standing there on that ground floor balcony with their radios were supervising what was going on in the village. That's also your position, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. From what I heard during that day, the radio contacts they had with their leaders, that told me that from that point they held everything under control. What was happening in Celina Krusha, and other villages. And they gave orders for nobody to go on that road, Celina-Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That is all in your statement, and we have that -- that wasn't a very good place to view the village from, was it? Couldn't see much of the village from there, could you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It was a very appropriate position, but of course it was impossible for us to see everything. But because we were there, there were moments when we could go close to the window and see what was going on in the courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm not talking about what you could see; I'm talking about those commanders. If they were directing what was going on in the village, that balcony that they were standing on was not a very good point to observe things from, was it? Ground floor balcony?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that misstates his testimony. I don't think he said "ground floor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He did actually say "ground floor," Mr. Hannis --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- in your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I misheard, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Whether that's wrong, you'll need to take up in re-examination, but he did say it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The balcony is about 3 metres from the ground level, so it was the first floor. You can see from the photograph that it's not on the ground level.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, even with that, it's not a good place to observe what was going on in the village, is it? You can't see the whole village from there, can you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't think that the commanders needed to see everything in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. My question is: You can't see the whole village from there, can you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: You can see most of it, 70 per cent of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, page 37, line 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My case manager pointed it out to me. I stand corrected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you and your cousin went into this attic, basically to hide, and you -- you already told me that it would have been very difficult for you to -- or impossible for you to stand up in that window and look out. So what did you do, did you kind of lie in front of the window and peer over it occasionally? Is that how you were able to see out of it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes we were lying down, and sometimes -- because we were stressed and because of what was going on, we went closer to the window. But we kept a distance from it, a safe distance, so that they could not see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, there were some soldiers who you say entered the house and came up to the floor immediately below you and to get a better perspective on that we should now look again at IC58 I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is IC58.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Oh, I keep getting them wrong, Judge. IC59.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So we can see the window where you were, and you say that just underneath that some soldiers came up there. And what you said about them was that: "They were stationed at the windows and appeared to be standing guard for the rest." Correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And they were immediately below you, on the floor immediately below you, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And how on earth could you see that they were stationed at the windows from up where you were?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: But there was this hole from which we could see them, and we could hear them talk, the observations they made. We could hear them. It was just below us. It's just 3 metres below us, and I can tell you -- I can mark here where they were. And they were there, to keep guard on the leaders that were in the other house, thinking that there was nobody in that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So what -- what is this hole you were talking about through which you could see them? I think you just made a blue mark next to some windows there. That would be where you claim the soldiers were looking out the windows I guess; is that true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The whole area of that floor, they would move around there, and they stayed there all the time that the commanders were staying where they were at the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, where is this hole through which you claim to have been able to observe them? So was there a hole in the floor?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, in the middle where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you could hear them very clearly I guess?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Because the sound was travelling between the two floors very easily, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. We could hear them very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In fact, what you said about that I think in paragraph 7 of your statement: "We could not make a noise while they were there, otherwise they would discover us." True?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So pretty difficult for you to even move around, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I guess we better have that captured and made an exhibit, Your Honour, so I -- because he put the little blue X there.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be IC62, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to go back again to the other one, which is either IC58 or IC59.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Make your mind up, John.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It must be IC58, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, can you show us where the school is?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can you show us where the school is? Where is the school in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It cannot be seen here. It's behind this house on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When you say "this house," do you mean the white house?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. That was the house where we used to live, where we were living. The school is at a distance from these houses into the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you can't see it from this spot?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: From this window where we were, from there you could see the school, but not in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this photograph is taken from the window where you were; that's what you told us.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not a photograph of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you couldn't see it from that window, could you, because it's behind that house there on the right that you say the commanders were standing on. So you couldn't see it, could you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Not from this window, but from various positions where we went, we could see the school when it was set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What do you mean from various positions where you went. You just told me you couldn't move without being discovered. You couldn't make any noise because they'd discover you.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: That was something we did -- we were able to move a little bit on tip toe in order to be able to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you could hear everything they were doing, you could hear them moving about, you could hear them talking, but you claim they couldn't hear you moving about in the attic up above them where there was a hole going through the floor?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you moved about, did you -- you must have gone completely to the other side of the house and looked out other windows. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There's only one window, of course, on that side of the house on that floor, isn't there?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Is there a window on the other end of that attic?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Did you go down to that end of the attic? Did you walk down there with these soldiers that could have heard you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, you couldn't see the school out the window on the other end of that attic either, could you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We saw the school from this window where we were. You could -- can see the school from here, but this photograph here, it's not very clear. We don't have a clear picture of the school. We were at this window, and we were following how the school was set alight.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you told me a minute ago you couldn't see the school from this window; now you can?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That doesn't accurately describe his evidence. His evidence is it's not in the photograph, but it's also to the effect that by moving into an appropriate position you can see the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's not what he said, Your Honour. At 55, line 5, he said, about the school: "Not from this window, but from various positions where we went we could see the school." So that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're quite right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could you tell us where it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you go back to 52, 22 you'll see: "From this window where we were, from there you could see the school, but not in this photograph."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he later agreed he couldn't see it from that window, but he could see it from a different position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I accept that, but there are different versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'll agree that we're both right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can clarify again. From the position of this window, you could see in the distance the school when it was set alight, but in this photograph here you cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I hunch what you're saying is that when the school started burning you could see the smoke coming up from the school and you knew that smoke was coming from where the school was. That's probably a fair statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. We saw the school and the smoke, and we saw the army that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. From -- from this vantage point that you had in this house, here's what you say in paragraph 8 of your statement: "Throughout the day, I saw soldiers entering and looting all the houses throughout the village. They would also remove the main part of the satellite dishes of all the houses. During the day 12 houses were burnt and then I remember that they burnt the school about 10.00 a.m. In the morning." Now, you couldn't see all the houses from there, could you? That's an exaggeration, that statement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Maybe it's from the notes that were different, but the looting and the robbing happened. Maybe not all the houses were seen, but most of the houses -- many houses I would say, and many houses were looted. But at that time I saw personally the school, how it was set alight, and the smoke came out. And there were other -- about 10, 12 houses that were also burned at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you were challenged about this in Milosevic by Judge Kwon - and I think this is at 6562 of the Milosevic transcript - explaining to Judge Kwon how it was possible for you to claim to have seen everything from this vantage point you said that while you were up there with those soldiers below you with a hole in the floor, that you could hear all the sound very clearly. What you told Judge Kwon was: "We could take away the tiles from the roof and be able to see what was happening around the village." Now, that can't possibly be true, can it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: That was true because where we were, on that floor, we were trying to create some space to see from those openings into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So there are these armed soldiers right below you that you're afraid of, and now you're moving all over that attic and raising roof tiles to look out. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, but of course we were very careful, and that was our ability. They did not dictate [as interpreted] we were there, they could not hear us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So your statement in paragraph 7 of your statement that: "We could not make a noise while they were there, otherwise they would discover us," simply isn't true. You could make a lot of noise; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, he didn't say he was making a lot of noise while he was doing that, Your Honour. It mischaracterises his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if it's not a reasonable inference, Mr. Hannis, from the evidence that there must be some noise. I think the criticism, Mr. Ackerman, is the use "a lot of noise" -- the expression "a lot of noise."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a moment, Your Honour, my computer has stopped working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, can I ask you meanwhile how you reached the roof tiles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was minimal height -- so that the soldiers would not hear us, the soldiers that were keeping guard downstairs, so we very carefully removed the tiles, 5 to 10 centimetres only, we moved them a little bit. So the noise was very slight, so the soldiers could not hear what was going on upstairs. We were very careful, extremely careful, because we knew that if they heard us it would mean death for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could we see IC59 again, please. Can you show us where the roof tiles are that you moved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The parallel side, on the opposite side, we lifted the tile a little bit and we could see the whole village. And you can see the road from Celina, Bellacerka, Krusha e Madhe, and from there we could observe everything that was going on in Celina. So we had to stand up, move the tile a little bit, and observe everything that was going on, the movements, the burning. From the X here, the window, you can see the school in the middle of the village because it's high up, so you can see the school from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Listen again, could you mark with the blue pen there the part of the roof where you moved the tiles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From this distance to the -- from here, it's 4 or 5 minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4 or 5 metres from here. That's where we removed the tile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we take a snap-shot of that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC63, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, do you want to go back to your exhibit, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No, I'm happy where we are, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, that window that has the red X on it we can see, that's the window from which the other photograph we've been looking at was taken, isn't it? I'm sorry, did you not hear me?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Where the red X is in this photograph, that's the window from which the other photograph we've been looking at was taken?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: IC58, and you took that picture, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'm wondering if you were up there taking pictures so we would understand what you could see, why you didn't raise up a roof tile and take a picture out through one of the roof tiles to show us what you could see in that direction.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Time was such that the security situation was very difficult, so it was not possible at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were up in the attic with your camera, you took one picture, but the security situation was so difficult you couldn't take two; is that what you want us to understand?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, let me suggest to you something more logical. It wasn't until you were challenged about your ability to see the rest of the village that you made up this statement about roof tiles, and that's why you didn't take a picture out of there that day, isn't it, because it didn't happen. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No, and I stated the same thing in the statement in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- Mr. Jemini, can you tell us when you took the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the photographs of the roofs, of the houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, the two photographs that we've been looking at, this one and the one taken from that window.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I took it after we returned to the village, during [as interpreted] the time that the Serb forces were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to move now to the next day, the 26th of March. We're at page 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that there is a not missing on line 62, "not during the time," he said, the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That puts a completely different --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- complexion on the answer. You said that you didn't take photographs from the -- from a gap in the roof because of the security situation. What was the difficulty at the time you took the photographs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were very much afraid we might be detected by the forces that were under us. We didn't want to make too much of a noise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're misunderstood my question. You took the photographs when you returned after the Serb forces had left, once you came back to your own home. And you suggested that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You also suggested that you limited the photograph taken to one from the window because there were security difficulties. Now, what were the security difficulties after you had returned home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't think it was appropriate to take other photos because we might have taken others as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So it had nothing to do with security, did it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Failing to take more photos from the window after we returned had nothing to do with the security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So I'm back to the prior question. You didn't do it because the story about roof tiles you made up after the fact, didn't you? That never happened, did it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes -- no. This happened during the time we were there hiding.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to go to the 26th of March, paragraph 16 of your statement -- it's actually the first full paragraph on page 4. You're talking about seeing a force approaching the village from the main road, and you noticed a troop carrier with 12 special forces police. You thought they were Arkan's men. You say they had long beards and shaved heads with no hats, similar uniforms and insignias as the soldiers from the day before, with red ribbons hanging from their left shoulders, similarly armed, but with large knives that were at least a half metre long. That's what you saw?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, the person that you were hiding in the attic with on the 25th of March was your cousin Isuf Jemini; correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And in your testimony in Milosevic you were asked if he also gave a statement to the Tribunal. Do you remember being asked that, at page 6559?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question once --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You were asked if he also gave a statement to the OTP, to this Tribunal. Do you remember being asked that question?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, at page 6559 of the Milosevic transcript starting at line 6, Mr. Milosevic asked this question: "You say that you were hiding for 48 hours in the attic with your cousin Isuf Jemini. Did Isuf give a statement to the investigators of the Tribunal as well?" Your answer was: "Yes, but given that the statement was fairly similar, given we were together all the time, it appeared sufficient to have only one statement of that kind submitted before this Tribunal." Now, that's what you said in Milosevic; was that true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. But then he was invited to come and testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, but when you say: "It appeared sufficient to have only one statement of that kind submitted before this Tribunal," to whom did it appear sufficient? Who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I was not told whether it was sufficient or not. We just gave the statements as we were asked to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, why did you say: "It appeared sufficient to have only one statement of that kind submitted before this Tribunal"? Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Because we thought it was sufficient since we were together. It was our own personal view.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, is it your position that you gave your statements on the same day?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Would it surprise you to learn that Isuf Jemini's statement was given on the 11th of June, 2002 - four days after you testified in Milosevic - that he had given statement? Would that surprise you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That wouldn't surprise you because when you said that in Milosevic, it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I think that whatever I said, it was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So when you said yes, that he'd given a statement to the Tribunal, that was true, even though I tell you now it was not given until four days later. Correct? For the Prosecutor it's K0227353?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: It is possible as what you are putting it to me, but I wasn't interested to know when he would give his statements prior to or after me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, weren't you interested in telling the truth when you were asked questions in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's questions don't assist this process. Mr. Jemini, in Milosevic you gave us -- you said clearly that Isuf Jemini had given a statement to investigators of the Tribunal. It's now being suggested that that was not correct. Now, why did you say in the trial of Milosevic that Isuf Jemini had given a statement to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time I had knew he had given a statement, but I had no knowledge as to when he gave the statement and when he acknowledged it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did you come to learn that he had given a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because when we gave statements in the village, he was there, too, often. But whether his actual statement was taken by the Tribunal or not, this I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if there is a statement preceding 11 June 2002 by Isuf Jemini, I would ask the Prosecution to produce a copy of it for me. But what has been produced so far does not include any statement earlier than 11 June 2002. So if there is such a statement, I would like to have it and I would end my cross-examination now with the right to resume it should I get that statement delivered to me at a later time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk -- oh, Mr. Visnjic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, I do have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, my name is Dan Ivetic, and I represent Mr. Sreten Lukic relative to these trial proceedings, along with my colleagues Branko Lukic and Mr. Ogrizovic. Now, I need to ask you a few questions today and I'd like to clarify some points made in your testimony and in your statements. Now, first of all today you clarified that the uniformed individuals that came into your village at 9.30 a.m. on the 25th of March were wearing green and brown uniforms. Can I take from that that it is your testimony that there were not any persons there at that time wearing blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I think we -- I explained it, that they had green camouflage uniforms. So the usual Serbian army uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ivetic, there is a supplement or an addendum to the statement, which I take it you've seen which is referring to that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked the question I asked, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can talk a little bit about another part of your statement, you describe towards the end of your statement, the last page as a matter of fact, at least in the English - I presume it's the last page in the witness acknowledgement in the Albanian as well - that bodies that had been along the roadway were collected and they were collected by persons you described as policemen with gypsies during the day. And I would like to ask you: Did both the men you describe as policemen and the men that you describe as gypsies wear uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The policemen, yes; the gypsies, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the uniforms worn by these men was solid blue in colour?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also described earlier in your statement - and I'm not sure whether it relates to your village or to one of the surrounding villages - but when you had left your position from the attic, you describe that you saw policemen with gypsies entering the village and stealing items from the village. Now, first of all, which village were you talking about at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Celina because we staid later for two months in Celina after the villagers had left it. During that period, every day they entered the village, looted it, and took away whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I can ask you, these persons that were with the gypsies, did they have the same uniforms as the individuals who were collecting the bodies that we have just talked about?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go back for a moment to the persons that were collect the bodies. Is it accurate that these persons travelled in trucks together with the individuals you describe as gypsies?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure. If we can go back for a moment to the persons in the solid blue uniforms that were collecting the bodies, is it accurate to state that these persons travelled in trucks together with the individuals you described as gypsies?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. As the mayor or president of your local community, as I think the official title is of your position, do you know about the existence of a municipal organ called the civil protection services?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And a few questions relating to -- a few questions relating to the individuals that passed by in the troop carrier that you referred to as the special forces police, the ones that you thought were Arkan's men. Now, when you say "special forces police," you're not talking about anyone who would be a member of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, are you?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: They belonged to MUP, too. They were part of Serbian forces involved in the massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, that's not what you say in your statement, is it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Which one are you saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the troop carrier of 12 special forces police that you said you thought were Arkan's men that had the long beards and the shaved heads with no hats, that came to your village, insulted your mother, and then continued onward toward Krusha e Madhe. Those people did not stay in your village. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: They went on. At that moment they didn't stop at our house; they just cursed my mother and went on their way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And so these persons that we are talking about were not present for the other events that you have testified about here today. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: On the previous day, no. One day earlier, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And so I'm -- my questions right now are focussed about these 12 individuals, because I'd like to get some clarification from you regarding about what you have said in your statement. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Those 12 policemen were not the same as the ones that I saw on the 25th in the village. They belonged to another unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the question I have for you is with respect to these individuals, they were not wearing the same uniforms as the persons you saw the prior day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to these persons here, these 12 individuals, did you have occasion to see anything on their uniforms with which you could identify them as being members of the MUP, the Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, on such occasions one cannot look at others very attentively because we avoided any possible contact, fearing death. So we couldn't -- I couldn't describe them in detail, but they were different from the prior ones because they had bandannas and they were wearing another uniforms compared to the previous day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The ones you are referring to the on the previous day, could you tell us what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The persons of the previous day were wearing different uniforms from the ones we are talking about. The later-day ones had bandannas, whereas the previous-day ones didn't. They didn't have knives, they didn't have ribbons, as the ones on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. But these questions are about police, and you indicated that there were police you saw on the 25th who were different from them. Now, what uniforms were the police you saw on the 25th wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those of the 25th were wearing blue uniforms as well as camouflage -- green camouflage uniforms of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I asked you earlier if in fact it was correct that there was no one wearing a blue camouflage uniform in the group that came to your village at 9.30 a.m. on March the 25th. How do you account for the departure from that testimony that you have now made?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I haven't said anything different. I'm telling the truth. On the 25th there are forces, military forces, wearing camouflage uniforms as well as -- green camouflage as well as police forces wearing blue uniforms. I'm talking about the 25th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is nowhere in your written statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor dated July the 17th, 1999, is it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: If it's not there, maybe they didn't ask me about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, what was the nature of the blue uniforms that you now say some of those present on the 25th were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the usual police uniform at that time, not the army, the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ivetic, you've ended up with a consistent position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Because your question was confined to blue camouflage uniform, and that may be part of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't believe it is, Your Honour, but I will explore that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but I think you do agree your question was confined to blue camouflage uniform at the beginning of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I think what we'll do is break now, since you're obviously not at the end of this, and we'll resume at 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jemini, we have to break now. The lunch break will be for one and a half hours, so you need to be back here to continue your evidence at 2.00. Meanwhile, you should not discuss any aspect of your evidence, either the evidence you've given already or the evidence you may yet give with any person. Talk about anything else with the people you're with at lunchtime, but you must not at any stage discuss the evidence. Now, could you please leave the courtroom, and you'll be shown where to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, the evidence will now continue. Mr. Ivetic will continue with his cross-examination. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I hope to be brief. I only have two areas to clear up and I'll return for the first part to these uniforms that were there at 9.30 in the morning on March, the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So now, sir, if you could please just confine our examination to this time-period so that there's no confusion. You testified before the break that there were police in this group. Now, I want to clear up a few things so I can tell exactly who we are talking about. In this group that came, this group of persons that came, there were green camouflage uniforms with an eagle patch, a double-headed eagle patch on the one hand, and there were police units on the other hand. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I think we're not understanding each other very well. On the 25th of March, the military forces had camouflage uniforms, while in that group of military forces there were also police with blue uniforms, blue clothes. So there were two groups. There is a military group and a police group, one with camouflage, one with blue, while the third group which is in the third phase, they were Roma and the police, but these were during the other days in the village. We have to be clear about these. This is my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to be clear and I'm trying to clear it up in my own mind as well as in the minds of everyone else here. Dealing with these groups -- this group that came at 9.30 in the morning and the group that you describe within there that were the police with blue uniforms, is it your testimony that these were solid blue uniforms or blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The uniforms were blue. The blue uniforms of the policemen, while the camouflage uniforms were the uniforms of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you that, about the camouflage uniforms; I asked you about the uniforms that you described as the police. Now, specifically with respect to these blue uniforms that you describe, what symbols or insignia did you see on those uniforms if any? That is to say, how did you come to the conclusion that they were police? Based upon what did you reach the conclusion that they were police?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Well, we know that because we lived in Kosova and we saw every day Serbian police, and they wore blue uniforms; that was the uniform of the Serbian police. I don't know what is not clear here. And they had the insignia of the Serbian police. You must know what those insignia are. I was not interested very much to see what the insignia were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, you said that I "must know what the insignia are." Why don't you tell us what the insignia are on the police uniforms that you saw. Describe them for us.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The double-headed eagle on the chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's on the persons in the blue uniforms that you saw?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now that we've cleared that up, let's move on to the group that came in the -- the 12 individuals that were talked about earlier that came in a troop carrier that only drove through your town. Okay. Can we focus on those now?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, with respect to these individuals, I believe you had already testified that you could not determine any type of insignia on their uniforms. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I did not see any kind of insignia. I saw only what I described earlier, that they had camouflage uniforms with red bandannas and also these knives in addition to the other weapons they were carrying.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And based upon what criteria did you label these 12 individuals as being police?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: We had experience from the past, from the operations that the army carried out and the other forces carried out in other parts of Kosova. So we were able to see directly what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: As I said, these were not the forces of the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This troop carrier that was carrying them did not have any markings of the Serbian police, did it?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: The troop carrier had markings, but we did not see what those marks -- those markings were. We just wanted to flee with our own lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right. And again, these troops continued down the road and did not take part in any of the events in your village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No. They moved on. From the place we were in the direction of Krusha e Madhe. Maybe they went to the centre of the village, but we don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions for this witness, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Jemini. My name is Djuro Cepic, one of the counsel for Mr. Vladimir Lazarevic. Today during your examination-in-chief we heard that you did your military service in 1988, and I presume that you wore the so-called Tito's cap, as did other soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement given to the OTP investigators on the 17th of July, 1999, at page 2, paragraph 4, you describe the soldiers who entered the village of Celina that day, and you say that they wore the so-called Tito's cap on their heads. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't think I said "Tito's cap." Military caps, yes, but I don't know what people would understand with this "Tito cap."

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Are we safe in this courtroom, having in mind the sound we just heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sure we're safe, Mr. Cepic, just --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't move.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your statement, as I said, on page 2, paragraph 4, you said that those who seemed to have been in command wore dark green berets, whereas the soldiers wore the so-called Tito's or Partizan-style cap, and they all had the same double-headed eagle insignia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, the double-headed eagle. The soldiers had camouflage uniforms, yes, but this Tito's cap, I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I can only quote your statement yet again, the one you gave on the 17th of July, 1999, in which you expressly state that the soldiers wore the so-called Tito's cap.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, in Serbian, the usual phrase is Tito's cap, and this is what Mr. Cepic keeps referring to, whereas in the statement we have the so-called Partizan-style cap.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my English says Partizan's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're told that the -- but the question that's being asked of you, Mr. Jemini, is about a phrase in your statement in which you say that the officers wore dark green beret-style hats and the soldiers wore the pointed Partizan-style hats. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Partizan style, yes, but I did not understand that Tito's cap, what was mentioned before. But yes, this Partizan style cap, I must have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify. They resemble the cap you must have been wearing while doing your military service. Wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Something similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I told you that in the Army of Yugoslavia, back from 1992, such caps were not in use altogether? What would be your comment as regards that, Mr. Jemini?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I don't understand what style cap you're saying that were not used after 1992. I did not analyse the kinds of caps that were used, whether they were Tito's or Partizan or what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's actually not true, Mr. Jemini, because your statement says clearly - and you've confirmed today that it's true - your statement says clearly that the soldiers at 9.30 on the 25th of March wore the pointed, Partizan-style hats. Now, do you wish to withdraw that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm saying that the soldiers, the Serbian soldiers that came on the 25th of March, who came at 9.00 in the morning, they had those caps. But as to this shape of Partizan or Tito's, I'm not sure about that. They were similar. I'm not sure about this even today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic is now suggesting to you that these pointed hats have not been worn since 1992, and he asked for your comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, because from 1992 I was not a member of the Yugoslav or Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Cepic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Two paragraphs below from the same statement you say that among the soldiers you recognised some as being from Rahovec. Is that correct, Mr. Jemini?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Those Rahovec soldiers, were they of 30 or 40 years of age, more or less; your peers, so to say?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know the names of some of the people you saw on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same statement, as referenced today, five paragraphs below. This is in the English page 3, paragraph 6; in the Albanian page 4, paragraph 2; and in the B/C/S, page 3, paragraph 5, you speak of commanders who used radio communication and inter alia you say that one of them said: "Don't let it happen the way it did in Racak." Do you know who participated in the Racak incident? Could you please answer with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. Mr. Jemini, on the 9th of January, 1999, do you remember a meeting in your village of Celina with Mr. John Fernandez, who was a senior officer for human rights with the OSCE mission, as well as another OSCE representative in Prizren, a Mr. Alex MacKenzie?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: You mean us or somebody else had that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You personally, in the village of Celina together with the two OSCE representatives you met?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: I can't remember. It could be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I can jog your memory by saying that on that occasion you expressed the uncertainty that could be felt with the villagers because the Army of Yugoslavia was setting up a check-point at the entrance of the village, and twice daily they would go to the check-point using an APC and some 25 soldiers. Wasn't that the main issue discussed at the meeting, Mr. Jemini?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, now I remember. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And at that meeting you said that the villagers were ready to support any actions by the so-called KLA as a response to this type of provocation unless the Army of Yugoslavia ceases to behave that way. You also stated: Rest assured that the soldiers will not advance because"they are afraid to enter the village." This is what you stated to these two gentlemen, didn't you, Mr. Jemini?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: If you could repeat the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As I said. The main topic was the VJ presence at a check-point at the entrance of the village, and then you stated that villagers, the inhabitants of Celina, were ready to support any KLA activity by way of response to the provocation unless the VJ ceases to behave this way. Then you continue: "In keeping with that, you can rest assured that the soldiers will not advance because they are afraid to enter the village."

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Everything was correct but what you said about the villagers, that they would support the KLA, that's not correct. The villagers asked that the check-point be removed from the village because it affected the situation in the area. The villagers answered that: We cannot guarantee what the situation be like if they intervene in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, I just have a few questions for you regarding where you were hiding in the house and where the commanders were on the balcony. Whether it was 12 metres away or twice or three times that distance, were you able to clearly hear the conversations?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the photo IC58 that we looked at, does that show all the angles from which you can look out that window?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you say you were able to see the schoolhouse from that window?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though it's not depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it you would have to move from the position the photographer was standing in to be able to see the school?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. We moved about in -- under the roof there in order to be able to see what happened in the whole village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ivetic at page 69, lines 6 through 9, asked you about civil protection services. Can you tell us, what did they do? What was their job?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: During the past ten years nothing was functioning with regard to civil protection in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So did -- were there any people assigned to that organisation or unit?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Not in the village, but maybe at the municipality level.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know what sort of work they were supposed to do in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: They had their own agendas. I don't know their agenda, but I would suppose to protect the population from the provocations and the pressure that was exercised on the population. But they did not carry out their duty to protect the population from the provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Lastly I want to re-visit the attic where you and your cousin were hiding. Mr. Ackerman asked you at page 63, lines 6 through 9 today, of -- a couple of questions. And you answered them both but I'm not clear. Did you really raise the tiles on the roof to get a look at what was happening around the village?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: Yes. We moved them a little bit so that we would be able to see what was going on in the rest of the village, because probably this is not clear to you. I would like to say, this is just a hundred square metres that we were situated. It was possible to move the tiles a little bit so that we could see other parts of the village. I apologise for this explanation that I added.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And so your answer to the question about whether or not you were making up that story about moving the tiles, what is your answer? Did you make that up?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jemini, I just want to ask you one thing. You referred to soldiers demanding money and your father saying that he had 12.000 Deutschemarks. What happened to the 12.000 Deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: AGIM JEMINI
utterances.text: When they were forced to leave the basement, my mother, my father, my uncle, his wife, and his son, they were asked whether they had money on them. My father said: Yes. And then they asked him: Where is the money? And they -- he said: I have the money in the bedroom in the house next to the house they were at. And he was accompanied to the room, to the bedroom. They got the money, and then they came back to the place where they were shot dead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Jemini, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give your evidence and to add to it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller has the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Lutfi Ramadani and he is a live witness. I'll just swap places with Mr. Hannis quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are we still in Celina?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We -- this witness is a survivor of a killing incident that is charged in paragraph 75(c) in the indictment and Schedule C. It's the village Krusha e Vogel, in Serbian Mala Krusa. And his evidence is also relevant to 72(a), 77 (a) and (b), and 25 to 32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to tell the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. We'll go straight into the questions that you'll be asked and the first person to question you will be for the Prosecutor, Ms. Moeller. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you please state your name for the record.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Lutfi Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And are you married?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you have children?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I have two children. I used to have four; two were killed. Now I have only two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Could you please spell your first name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lutfi Ramadani, from Krusha e Vogel village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough. All the documents have it spelled wrong, I think, but it's correct now, it's corrected in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, where did you live in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: In Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how big was your village at the time, how many inhabitants were there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It had 70 households and 800 inhabitants. 112 have been shot and burned.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was the ethnic composition of your village in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: In 1999 they surrounded us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I think maybe my question was not clear. Krusha e Vogel in March 1999, did only Kosovo Albanians live in your village or also Serbs?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were also Serbs along with the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were there other ethnicities as well?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were Romas, two households of Romas.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was the relationship between the Albanian villagers and the Serb villagers and the other two households of Romas which you mentioned before the 24th -- yeah, the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From 1989 or 1990, our relationship was good with everyone. From 1999 or 1990 [as interpreted] the situation started a little to be worsened. We didn't have any quarrels, any problems among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And now I would like to talk with you about the 25th of March, 1999, the day after the NATO air campaign started. In the morning of the 25th March 1999, what did you observe in your village Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, at 4.00, we saw that we were surrounded from all sides with tanks and anti-aircraft artillery weapons, armoured cars. The road that goes to Prizren-Gjakova was full of tanks and such artillery weapons. The armoured cars came to the village streets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how far away is the road that you mentioned between Prizren and Gjakova from the centre of the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It goes to the village -- it goes through the village or at the edge of the village. There are houses on both sides of the street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did you also see any persons who would man these vehicles in this morning?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: My house is at the outskirts of the village from where you can see the Prizren-Gjakova road, and I saw the tanks, the anti-aircraft parked there. And in the streets of the village, as I said, there were armoured cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did anyone enter your village from the outside who arrived with these vehicles? Did you see any uniformed persons coming into your village that morning?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, there were. At the edge of the village from the asphalt road, some vehicles came and stopped there, whereas the army was stationed besides the asphalt road. The militia entered the village, they entered the houses and started setting them on fire and shooting.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did the people that you called the militia look? How were they dressed? Which kind of uniform, if any, did they wear?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They had black uniforms but also other uniforms. They could wear whatever clothes they wanted and wished. There wasn't a single type of uniforms -- uniform. There were several.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you describe the several kinds of uniforms that you saw in your village that morning?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were black and camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the camouflage uniform, which colour did they have?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think I answered your questions. I said black and multi-coloured camouflage. I didn't pay any close attention to the colours, to tell you the truth, because our main concern was to escape.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Did you note at this time also some local persons in uniform who you would know from your village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. They were from the village. There were others who we didn't know, but those from the village were in the lead. They told them where the houses of Albanians were, and they entered these houses and set them on fire immediately. When they started shooting and set fire to the houses, then the people began to leave the houses and to flee the village. We went to a stream, and we stayed there in the house of Adem --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, these local people that you just referred to, what did they wear?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The clothes of the militia, but there were also people without uniforms. They had some bandannas on the heads, white and red, like ribbons tied on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Among the local Serb people, do you recall any particular persons? You know the names of who were among them?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Nikolic Dimitrije, Nikolic Ranko --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, is the witness reading right now?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: No, there is no paper in front of him, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to be clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Mr. Ramadani, with the names that you can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nikolic Momcilo, Nikolic Sava, Thaqi Sreto [phoen], Djordjevic Zlatko, Cvetkovic Djordje, Petkovic Ranko, they were in uniform and armed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And which colour had their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The uniform of the militia, black.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Had you seen any of those people you just listed, seen wearing this uniform or any uniform before that day?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were there sometimes some months ago, sometimes in uniform, sometimes without uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you just said that they were leading the other persons that you did not know into the village, showing them the houses. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, together with them. They were together, those whom we knew and those we didn't. They entered the houses together on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what did they do in the houses?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They set them on fire, especially those houses that were situated on the side of the asphalt road, they set them on fire on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You already mentioned that you and the population of the village fled after that happened or when that happened. Where -- where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We went to the stream of Adem Isufi. It is not very far from the village, I would say. We stayed there only one day. On the 25th when night came at 7.00 it became cold because there were elderly women and men, young children, babies, newly born babies, and then we went to the house of Sejdi Batusha and we spent one night there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How many people were with you in these woods?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I couldn't count them, about 500, more than 500.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did all of the people return in the evening to the village or did some stay in the wood overnight?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We returned, almost all returned, with the exception of two families which remained there. Liman Hazeri, with his wife, son, and Nebi Hazeri with his wife, son.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during the stay that you spent hiding in the woods, what did you observe going on in Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We heard firing, firing which none of the shots hit anyone from the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we call up Exhibit P99, page 1, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, we're calling up a picture on the screen in front of you, and I would like to have you have a look at this picture, at this photo. Can you see the photo on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you see on this photo approximately the woods where you were hiding that day?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The usher will give you a pen and if you could -- if you could draft an A where you were hiding.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I can. This is the forest here where we hid, here. The photo doesn't show all of it because the place where we stayed is here at this corner. There is a stream here where we hid.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the witness made a mark in the very left corner of this photograph, depicting the approximate area where they hid in the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you also said that when you returned in the evening that you went to a specific house. Could you say again whose house that was?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The house of Sejdi Batusha. It's not in the photo here. There is a vineyard here, they belong to Sejdi Batusha.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You do not see the Sejdi Batusha house on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It's here, above the road, not the first one but this one. There are three houses here in line, but the photo doesn't show it very well because there was another house here at the corner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we maybe take a snap-shot of this one and then zoom in a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC64, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And then zoom in, in the left area of the houses which are a little bit outside of the main village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Now it's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you assist with the pen one more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, do you think you can mark the house here?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can see it very well now. This is the oda or the guestroom. There was a two-storey house here, and this house here, it's okay, this is how it was. These are the houses of Sejdi Batusha, and this belongs also to Sejdi Batusha.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
