utterances.text: Could we take a snap-shot of this picture, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC65, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Batusha [sic], how many people were in this house in the night between the 25th and the 26th March?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the 25th of March, in the evening, we went there. We entered the oda and the women entered other rooms. All of us, about 500, with the exception of the two families that did not return, all of us went into those rooms. On the next day, on the 26th, we walk and went out in the yard. It was about 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. And what did you see this morning? What was the general situation in the village this morning?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We woke up at about 6.30 or 7.00. I'm not sure about the exact time. At about 8.00 we heard firing again. The Serbs from the village with the help of other Serbs started to open fire and loot and raid the houses, taking away the most valuable things, tractors or cars, and then after they removed all the valuables they set fire to the houses, while they were burning the houses and -- they were approaching the population. In the meantime Isen Kanjusha who lives near Sejdi Batusha went to set free the cows to send them to graze, and he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, just to clarify. You referred to the other Serbs who were together with the Serb locals. Were -- how did these other Serbs look, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were dressed in the police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened next then after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we have a name for the person who was killed, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the name of the person you said was killed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Isen. Ramadani is his last name, but he called him Isen Kanjusha.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how was he killed, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: He was killed from the Boshki [phoen] or Seka's [phoen] house, he was killed by the Serbs who shot him from that house.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you know the full name of this Boshki or Seka?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Stankovic Bosko, this is how we called him because their names are different from ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And the Serbs who shot him from this house, who were they? Did you know them from before?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were not far. We were here in this courtyard. Isen Kanjusha's house is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, I think you didn't answer the question. Did you -- did you also recognise the people who shot or were these people who were not from the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We didn't see them from where they shot. We saw them that they shot from the balcony, but we couldn't say who they were because it's more than 200 metres away from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, you said you were standing in the yard together with the other people. Were you approached by anyone at any time that morning?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were setting fire to houses and they were approaching, so this is Milaim Batusha's house and then Liman and Sait's house. And in this last house where they came they removed the tiles and they put the barrels of their guns there. They also went to another house and they took position at the windows. Because of the fear, because of these things that were happening, the women were so scared, terrified, and some of them fainted. We couldn't help anybody because no one would allow us to help these people who fainted. So somebody called a volunteer Aziz Shehu was called. He was told to go to the mountain and to the stream and call the people who were hiding there, and he came back with Liman Hazeri, his son was paralyzed, and they came back where we were, where the population was, and they ordered us to leave all our clothes here and leave, go out on the main street, women in a group and men in another group.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. Who sent Aziz Shehu to collect the people from the woods who were still hiding there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Who called Aziz there? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who told Aziz that he should get the people out of the woods and back into the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Okay, yes. The ones that were at Milaim's house, the policemen who were at Milaim's house. I did not see them because the curtain was down, but it was them who ordered him to go and collect those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when all those people were then collected and assembled in the yard, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: When they came to the yard, the order was to go out on the street, women separately from men. Some of the children went with women, those who were 15 years old and under.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And who gave those orders?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The order was given by the police from Milaim's house. Some of these policemen were not known by the people, we did not know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what happened to the women then after they were ordered to assemble in one group with some of the children?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The children who were under 15 years old went with the women, and Cvetkovic Djordje ordered the policemen to go to the women, and those children who were 13 years old and up to be brought to the men. So they went there. The women wouldn't let their children go. They started to use force, and women were so frightened some children were let go then. It was about 14 children. Among those -- my son was among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this Cvetkovic Djordje is a man that you mentioned earlier today and you said all of a sudden he was also wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. He was wearing a uniform, Cvetkovic Djordje.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were Cvetkovic Djordje and the other men, were they saying something to the children?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, no. They were staying at Milaim's house. It's above there. They just told other policemen, these were unknown policemen to us, and they went to the women.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did they say anything to the women?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Who do you mean? The policemen, the unknown policemen? I'm sorry, maybe my question was really unclear. I rephrase that. After the women were assembled together with some children, this group, what were they ordered to do.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The women were crying: You took our women -- you took our men, you're taking our children away. What can we do? And they told them: Go to Albania. When the women were leaving, we were ordered to -- to take off our clothes and put our hands up on our heads.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. After the women -- just to make this clear for the Honourable Judges, after the women were told, "Go to Albania," did they leave the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Either go and drown yourself in the Drini River or go to Albania, and then they took the road to Drini. When they left, we did not see them anymore, but the women can testify themselves where they went.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Was your wife in this group of women?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, my wife was in that group. And my daughters-in-law, all the women in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after the group of women had left towards the direction of the Drini River, what did the policemen tell you, the group of men, to do?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were told to kneel down, put our hands up. Some policemen in uniform came, and they ill treated us. Some of us were beaten. They asked us to give them our wallets, money, documents. Adem Isufi was ordered to collect all the documents and the money and give the money to them. Then another group came. There were people in masks in that group, but also people without masks. They swore a little bit, but they didn't beat anyone. They left. They asked for the car keys. They got the car keys. And after this we stayed there for a little while. We were ordered to stand up and line up in threes and walk towards the road. And we were led to Qazim Batusha's gate. We turned right and went to the barn, Qazim Batusha's barn.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Let me stop you here shortly to clarify some issues.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: First of all you said the second group of persons who came and who wore masks, did they also wear uniform or other clothes?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, they had uniforms and masks. Generally the people -- those people had uniforms, but some of them, a couple, two or three of them, had masks on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And what colour have these uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The same, black.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now I would like to talk with you a little bit about the men in this big group. How old was the youngest in this group, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: 13 years old to the elderly, 75.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how many under-aged persons were in this group, approximately?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were about 14 under 15-year-olds there were more under 18, but I didn't count them. But I counted the ones under 15, who were 14, and I wrote them down.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And was there more than one elderly person in this group?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were a lot of elderly people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And were all the men in this group healthy persons or was there anyone with disabilities?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were two mentally disabled. There were two other people who were paralyzed, Liman and Sait Hajdari, while the ones who were mentally disabled were younger. One of them was called Bekim.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to call up Exhibit P99, page 1 again, please. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think it's on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you. Can we zoom in maybe a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a little bit, please, yes. If you could enlarge it a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think -- would that be --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, he needs his glasses to look at that closely.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, can you see --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Could you hold on for just a minute?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, now I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: If you can, I would like you -- you already marked earlier the house where the yard was where you were assembled. And now I would like to mark you, if you can, the road that you were marched down to the Batusha barn that you already mentioned, you and all the other men.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This route, here we were divided. We took a turn here and there are two big holes here. It was here. There are two holes. This is the destroyed house, and after the war only these two holes are here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The two holes -- sorry, the two dots that you put on, just to clarify, that was where the Batusha barn was standing, where you were marched to that day?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, it's a barn -- a cowshed where he kept his cows and also food.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Is that clear for the record, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, could you also draw a red line back to the house where you were coming from, in the yard of which you had been assembled when the march started.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: From here, yes, this is the house of Sejdi Batusha. From here.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: My hand is trembling a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That's very understandable, sir. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: May the record reflect that the red line drawn is the way that the men were taken down to the barn.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can we take a snap-shot of this picture, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC66, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, you already mentioned that it was a kind of a cowshed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could the OTP give a time reference when this photograph was taken? I believe it would be very helpful, and it could be done at a later stage. It needn't be done immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know the answer, Ms. Moeller?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think it was taken in summer 1999, but I would like to verify the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you already mentioned it was a kind of a cow stable, that building. How many rooms had it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Two rooms and a corridor. There was some hay, some fodder there, that was all there was there when we entered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And did all the 110 men enter this cowshed, these two rooms and the corridor?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: 109, we entered the cowshed, while 103 remained there, they were executed and burned. Six survived, and we are alive to this day. But we don't know where the remains of the rest are, where the Serbs of the village took them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ramadani, when you were all in this -- in this cow stable, in the cowshed, did you hear the policemen who escorted you there say anything?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were several policemen. There were many along the road when we were walking, some we knew, some we didn't. But two of them got into the corridor. We were packed in that corridor, and they told us, some people, to go to one room, others to go to the other room. Myself, I stayed in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were also physically disabled men with you. Were these men able to walk or how did they get to the cowshed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were inside as well. I said they were mentally disabled. They were -- their psyche was not -- they had psychological problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sorry, was there anyone in this group in a wheelchair?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, Sait Hajdari was in a wheelchair and also Avdyl Limani [phoen] was also paralyzed and he had to be carried.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where was the man in the wheelchair in the stable, in which room were where in the corridor?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Sait Hajdari was at the doorstep. When I got out of there, I pushed him a little bit. He was killed. He was covered in blood. I had to push him a little bit in order to be able to go out.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ramadani, when you were all in that -- all assembled in that cowshed, what did the policemen do to all the men there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The policemen were staying outside. Some of them were guarding us. Then other policemen came. I did not see them; I couldn't. I saw this policeman who had a machine-gun, and the other one said: "Why are you late?" And this one said: "Well, I'll take care of it now." And he opened fire. It was non-stop fire until he finished all his bullets. And then they came with a rifle and whoever who could raise their heads, they shot them single shots. I heard single shots. And then they set the place on fire. People started to burn. I started to burn. Then I slowly began to go out. It was six people. We got out. Some went to the meadow. I went in the direction of Krusha e Madhe. This was non-asphalted road, and there were blood traces on the road, but we were shot. We were shot from the asphalted road again.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, you -- how did you leave the barn, through which -- which way? Did you leave it through the entrance door or through any of the windows?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I left through the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when you came out of this barn, did you see and recognise anyone in the vicinity of the barn?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them on this road here that goes down. They were talking. There was some policemen talking to each other, but I think there was some civilians as well because I was trying to get away from there, to save my life. So it was me, Agim, and Bajram, we got out of there. Some went down, some -- along the houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And in this group that was standing close to the barn or on the village road, you said, was there any of your co -- Serb co-villagers that you knew?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were Serbs from the village, but there were other policemen that we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you recall who of the Serb villagers were there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There was Boshki, Cveta, Bushki [phoen], et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: What would be the full name of Boshki, please, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Stankovic Bosko. His house is right here, very close. Seka is Stankovic -- Stanko Nikolic, and the other one is Rade Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who is Bushki?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Cvetkovic, Cvetkovic Bosko.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, were you injured in this shooting and burning of the Batusha barn?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was not hit by a bullet, but I was burned, this side of my body, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when -- in the moment you made it out of this cowshed, did you know of all five other survivors being alive or how many did you actually see yourself?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: At that time I saw Petrit, he was alive. He was leaning on the wall. He was feeling the way along the wall, and his cousin -- but then he was killed at the stream Qamil Shehu, but he left a little later, while myself, Bajram, and Agim, we left together, all of us three.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Sir, were you -- two of your sons in the group with you in this cowshed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. My two sons, my brother and his son, they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You said "they remained there." To your knowledge, did they survive this incident?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, they were burned. They were burned. 80 per cent of the people I think died because of the flames. Only 20 per cent died because of the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: How old was your younger son who died there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: 14 and a half.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how old was the other one?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how old was your brother?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And your nephew, how old was he?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: By nephew was 28 years old.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And can you also give us the names of your four relatives?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: My sons, the youngest was called Bajram, the other one Afrim. Afrim Ramadani and Bajram Ramadani. My brother Murat Ramadani and his son, Selajdin Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: When you managed to flee from the stable, in which direction did you flee?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I went along this road. It's a road that goes towards Krusha e Madhe. It's not asphalted, that road. From the asphalted road, we were shot at, and we were not able to walk further, so we went down the stream and then into the forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I notice the time. I still have a couple of questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what's your estimate of the time for these questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Maybe 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. We'll break just now then and we'll resume in half an hour. Mr. Ramadani, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Could you please go with the court usher; he'll show you where to wait until we resume.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue, Mr. Ramadani. Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, we stopped at the point after you had managed to leave the Batusha barn and to flee along the stream. After you did so, did you return to the vicinity of your village, Krusha e Vogel, in this week?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I stayed for ten days in the mountains of Krusha e Vogel.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during this time, what could you observe going on in -- in and around Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There wasn't much I could see because I was in the forest; during the day I stayed there and I moved about at night. I could hear [as interpreted] the stench of dead bodies and because of the burning houses it was very difficult to breathe in the stream where I was staying. But as for seeing, it was very little I could see. I could see some movements of the Serbs. The army and the police left.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You say movements of the Serbs, army and police, do you refer to army vehicles or to -- what kind of movements did you see?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I mean the vehicles, they left. The vehicles of the army, they left after two or three days, they left the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after you had stayed in the vicinity of your village for about ten days, what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Then I went to -- to Drini and I stayed in Bjeshkat e Hasit for another five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And where did you stay there, did you stay in the village or did you still stay in the woods?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: In the woods.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how would you feed yourself during these weeks?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: At night we went to some houses, found something to eat there, and like this we managed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: You say "we." Were you in the company of someone else?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We were four people.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Who else was with you there?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Bajram Zylfiu was with me. He was one of the survivors of that massacre, there was also Gani Zulfiu and Safet Berisha.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: These other two men, apart from Bajram Zylfiu, where were they from, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were from Krusha e Vogel, too; they were neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Were they also survivors of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, they were not survivors. They were not mountains. We met by accident. Myself and Bajram were the two survivors. They had left the village before the massacre, these other two. They wanted to escape falling into the Serbs' hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And during that time that you were in the woods, these weeks, did you find any way to treat your burn wounds on your arm?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We tried to treat it by some popular, let's say, medicine like yoghurt. We used some yogurt.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Where did you get this yogurt from?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We went to some houses in Has, on the other side of Drin, and we found this yogurt that the population had left behind. It was sour yogurt and that was what I used to treat my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Was there any population around when you went to these villages to get food and treatment or were they --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, no, there was no one left because the people had fled. They had gone to Albania. The houses were deserted.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, when you came to The Hague this week, did you provide a list of names to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what list do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P2357, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: A document which contains the names of the men who were killed in the Batusha barn and some other names?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. These are the names of the village inhabitants which I prepared, and then when that happened I drew from the list the names. I have a list of 39 people of Shehu family; then come Batusha family, 22 people. I apologise but Shehu -- from the Shehu family, five didn't leave their houses and they are found in another list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you have a look at this document which is on the screen, and see where this is the document that you provided to us this week?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I think so, must be it. Nuredin Qazim Shehu, Sefer Nuredin Shehu, yes, yes, that's the right list.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And this is a typed-up document. Who typed in document?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, it is typed. I typed it. I wrote it in fact by my hand and then went somewhere else to have it typed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And when did you first draft up the handwritten list, which is the basis of this document, the names?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I drew up this list immediately after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when? Was it in 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: After 1999, when the investigators came to take the notes, this is when I prepared -- maybe it was a little -- a while after them, after they came. But at that moment I wasn't feeling very good. I couldn't concentrate very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And do you -- do you maintain that all these men who are listed on page 1 and two of this list were men who were with you in the Batusha barn and who have not been seen since?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. They were not seen ever since, and to this date we don't know of what happened to their remains. But maybe the accused and their Defence lawyers know where the remains of these people are found.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could I also ask you to have a look at page 3 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3, please? I think this is page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The next page, please. I would need the next page. Yes. Could we zoom in a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, the first five names on this list, are these the men who survived this massacre, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. These people are alive to this day, and they are the survivors of that massacre.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And could we scroll down, please? Further.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The last eight names at the bottom of the list --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Are these local people from your village whom you saw participating that day in the events in your village and who we talked about, some of them, earlier today?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, they are local Serbs from our village, whom I mentioned earlier Dimitrije, Ranko, Momcilo, and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And could we scroll up a little bit again to see the middle part?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ramadani, the nine persons who are listed in this part, who are they?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: These are from our village, but these are people who did not leave their houses, thinking that nobody would harass them. But they were burned at home, all of these persons. Nine people. We found them, only their skeletons burned, and then we buried their skeletons.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Actually, Your Honour, I think that we have some objections regarding this document, but I don't think that you want to hear them now. Or you do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, what is your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I saw this document 15 minutes ago for the first time; and the second thing is that these, for example, nine names, I think have never been mentioned before and this is the first time we saw these names. We were not able to do any kind of investigation on this part, and it's not in 65 ter motion either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I assist maybe to clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The nine names that we talked about just now, the nine additional people who the witness says were killed and were burned in houses, they are indeed not in Schedule C, and I just had this addressed for completeness. As to the provision of the document, the witness brought it only when he arrived at the Tribunal, which was very late in the week, according -- pursuant to some visa problems. And we provided it early this morning to the Defence, and we only received it yesterday de facto. Last night we sent supplemental information that such list had been provided and that names had been put forward, and we would wish to tender the document as far as it concerns the names of the people who died according to the witness in the same killing incident that he survived and with regard to the Serb persons named in the document, which he also referred to earlier in his testimony, and with regard to the survivors to make the record complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. This document is of the nature of an aide-memoire in relation to evidence that the witness could give orally. There is no question of a conviction being sought in respect of the nine names in the middle of page three. In these circumstances, it's appropriate to admit this document to explain the evidence in a form that's easily read by everyone. Obviously, if the Defence demonstrate in due course any prejudice as a result of the late intimation of this document, albeit the information generally contained and it was available to them, then we would consider any application to remedy the prejudice.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I have a question. Can I ask it, please? They were burned on the 25th, because when the police entered they didn't leave their houses and they were burned inside the houses. I am -- I have testified for 103 people, and I'm still testifying for 103 people. But the nine persons, as I am explaining to you, were killed or burned at home. I was not among them. I was among the 103 persons that I am testifying for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, we have that; we're clear about it. And this doesn't affect your evidence in any way. We have the whole picture before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is clear for -- to all of us I think. Thank you. When did you return to your village, Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: On the 15th of June. Maybe I'm not very accurate about the date. I know for sure it was June, but it might have been 18th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did the village look when you returned?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It was in a pitiful condition. All the houses were burned. It was a very desperate view to look at. Not a house was -- not a single house was intact. Some were -- only the roofs were burned. Some were burned in other parts, but the entire village was burned, I mean the houses of Albanians, not the houses of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: That is the point I wanted to clarify with you. So it was only the Albanian houses that were burned. How did the Serb houses look?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They were quite intact when we returned from Albania.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how did the two households of Romas, these two houses look, in what state were they in?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They, too, were in good condition because they were together with the Serbs in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And after you returned to your village, did you also go back to the Batusha cowshed at some point?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I went immediately to see, but cowshed was blown up. It was built with concrete blocks, but all had been scattered all around and there were only two pits left of them. We found some burned shoes and some sleeves, some pieces of clothes, nothing else, because excavators had been -- bulldozers had been working before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we call up Exhibit P100, page 3, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, is that -- can you identify what is on this picture, on this photo?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. The two holes, two pits nearby this house, but when they blew up the two -- the cowshed, this house, too, was blown up. It was destroyed, I mean. So now you can see only two pits, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can we have the same exhibit, page 4, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Talking about pits, is that one of the pits that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, this is the pit or the hole that I am talking about, but there is another one. Here was the corridor and the two rooms. Instead of the rooms there are the two holes or pits and you see the concrete blocks thrown all over.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to show you one last photograph, and that is Exhibit 101, page 1, please. Mr. Ramadani, we talked about one of your co-villagers, Sait Hajdari, who was confined to a wheelchair and him being in the cowshed as well. Could you have a look at this picture which is upcoming. Now --

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't see any -- yes, now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Can you have a look at this wheelchair?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, the wheelchair belonged to him, to Sait Hajdari. But Shez [phoen], his wife, but I had not seen her because they lived far from me, but I know that the wheel belonged to Sait.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, do you know a British journalist called John Sweeney?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Maybe I know him. There were many journalists.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you talk to journalists in -- close to the events, close after the events after you returned to Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: After the event in Krushe, there were many foreign journalists, but as I said I wasn't feeling so well and I didn't take down their names, and so I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Do you recall any journalists with a film crew coming into your village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Many journalists came, but I kept away because I was suffering from a trauma at that time and I didn't want to get involved. But what I went through, I told the journalists, but I didn't write down their names. I know that it was Petri and John.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, I have only two questions left. How is the village of Krusha e Vogel today?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We have received a lot of aid from internationals and the house now is in good condition, not as good as it should be, but compared to the state we found it, it's much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And how is the situation for the children in Krusha e Vogel today?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The situation for the children is not good because the number of children has been reduced, and we found out now that we sent the children to school. We used to have 28 to 30 kids per class. Now we have only 14, and you can see that their number has diminished.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And -- I'm sorry, please continue.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: We have 80 women with husbands. We have 52 women who have orphan children.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: And my very last question: How is your personal condition today, Mr. Ramadani?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Not very good, but I'm trying as far as I'm able to walk. Sometimes I feel nervous and I kind of start shaking because of what I went through at the time of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your patience, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: This completes my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ramadani, which parts of your body were burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The right part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your body as well as your arm?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. My arm, my hand. You can see the marks on my hand, but the part on the arm, it has healed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your left hand, was it also burned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No because I fell on my left side of the body, but it was the right side that caught fire, my clothes as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, I've just a question for you. Now, things are becoming normal in your village and you say that the -- because of the aid you have been able to build-up the house and children are also going to school. But, as according to you, the number of children have reduced. So it doesn't give the hustle bustle of life. But what I would like to ask you is: How are the inter-ethnic relationships now after the -- after this post-era of the incidents you have mentioned? How are you interacting and how is this relationship existing between different ethnic groups and yourself? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what ethnicities do you mean now? There are no more Serbs in the village. There are some Romas in the village, but they live further away. We have good relations with them, no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: What about villages close to you, not really your own village if your population is overwhelming. What about other villages next door where you may be having Serbs, what type of relationship do you have with them, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No relations at all because they are far away. Some of them are in Rahovec and it's far away, so I have no connection with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: But you must be meeting them off and on going here and there at marketplaces far away collecting bric-a-brac or other things. How is the behaviour how and how you feel yourself amidst them now after you have rehabilitated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't go to the market. I work as a farmer. I'd like to tell you: If your son gets killed, what can you think about that person? I don't think you would think well of such a person. If your sons get burned in front of your -- of you, just right before your eyes, I don't think you would think well of such a person who does that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the order is: General Lukic, General Pavkovic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lazarevic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ramadani. My name is Branko Lukic, and I would kindly ask you to assist us in clarifying certain points?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I'd like the assistance of the registrar to be able to see P99 on the screen, page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadan, on this photograph - and with the assistance of the usher - could you please mark the house of Bosko Stankovic from which fire was opened at Hyseni.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I can show you, no problem. This is Bosko's house. This is Ceka's house, and this is Milos's house. So Boski's, Ceka's, and Milos's, and this is Hysen Ramadani's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... record, Mr. Lukic. Which one is the one that you're after, Bosko's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just next to Bosko's house, could you please put the number 1.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Number 1, here, is Ceka's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then please put 2 next to Bosko Stankovic's house.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Oh, yes, Boski's; this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: The figuration is not very correct, visible. Could the usher also help him, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's clear, so 1 is 1, 2 is 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... middle one of the three is number 1 and the one on the left is number 2. Just one other thing, just to be absolutely clear, would you also mark with a 3 the house of Hyseni Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, should we admit this as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be IC67, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, today we heard that the reason of people leaving your village was because policemen in black uniforms surrounded your village. How many policemen were there? Can you tell us that?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I couldn't count how many policemen there were because it wasn't to see from here to there, so we couldn't see all of them. They were in groups, several groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a circle that was created around the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. I told you earlier that the village was surrounded by the army. The army was in the mountains and around the village and on the road, while the police were in the streets of the village, inside, while the population went to seek shelter in the stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's why I was asking you this question. Provided the village was encircled, how did you manage to leave the village and go to the forest?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Well, they did not do anything to the people who were leaving and going towards the forest. This is the route we took to this field here and then to the forest, but they did not allow people to go in the other direction. But they allowed people to go towards the mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And all this took place around 4.00 or 5.00 a.m.; is that so?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure, it was about 5.00, yes, around that time. At 4.00 we saw that we were surrounded and the people began to leave their homes at about 5.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we conclude then that among the policemen there were no policemen wearing blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It was not a problem for them because they could change their clothes whenever they wanted. Blue, black, or camouflage, they had all these uniforms. I'm talking about the village here, and I'm saying that whatever they thought appropriate they did. And they put on the uniforms that they wanted. So when they began to set the houses on fire, the first houses on fire, and when we heard the shooting, we left our houses and went to the stream. And we did not look back because in fact from the stream you cannot see what's going on up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. I just wanted to ask you whether you want to change your testimony now, since you said during your cross-examination that there were -- or rather, I wanted to ask whether -- do you not want to change your testimony to the effect that there were some other uniforms apart from the black ones you testified about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he gave evidence earlier that there were camouflage, multi-coloured uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but black, black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Indeed he said black and camouflage uniforms, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All I'm saying is you have to put the question on an appropriate basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramadani, at page 7, line 15 of today's transcript, you said: The police entered the village and started setting fire to the houses. They wore black uniforms and camouflage uniforms. Were these two different types of uniform?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I did not say "camouflage uniforms." As I explained earlier, I did not sit there and watch what kinds of uniforms they were wearing or changing into. We went to the stream. The uniforms, they know about the uniforms. And I think that the uniform is not important. The damage that was caused is important and who caused that damage? The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, please don't try to decide yourself what's important; it is for the Court to decide what's important. And while it may be clear beyond any doubt that a large number of people were killed here, what we are concerned about is who is responsible for that. And to help us to try to identify who is responsible, then we need information about what they looked like, if that information is available. And that is why you're being asked these questions. So be in no doubt that these are important questions. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Why am I asking you all this? And why did His Honourable Judge Bonomy issue these instructions? This is so that you can tell us that you don't know something or that you may not be certain of something, provided that is so. It is a legitimate answer, by all means.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I'm sure about the police, that they had black uniforms; and the army that was around on the main road and on the mountains, that they had the tanks and the anti-aircraft artillery weapons. I'm sure about those.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. As we have heard already, there were some Serbs in your village. Were any of them fully employed with the police, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who of your co-villagers was fully employed by the police?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Petkovic Cedomir was there, also Nikolic Rasko, then Nikolic Momcilo, Cvetkovic Dragi. These ones were the local ones. Nikolic Ranko, Djordjevic, Djordje Cvetkovic, Sava Nikolic, Tasic Cveta, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any reserve policemen in your village, Serb reserve policemen?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was employed, and from 1992 I left the job, and there were new people there. There were reservists and regular police, but the ones that I mentioned were regular police. The reservists, sometimes they had their uniforms on, sometimes they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any members of local security forces in your village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: What security do you mean, security of the village or the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Local security, local guards, people from your village who were in charge of security.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I said that -- was this about the Serbs or the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Either, Mr. Ramadani.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Nikolic Dimitrije had a cafe, and they drew up their plans there. The Serbs always used to gather there and had meetings there, drew their plans, but people from other villages came as well, not only from Celina. But there were no guards --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, you said that you were employed and from 1992 you left the job. What was that job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in Prizren at a factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And at that stage did you leave the village or did you stay in Celina -- sorry, in Mala e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in Krusha e Vogel and I commuted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, in 1998 and 1999, were there any Albanians employed with the police?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, there weren't. There maybe were Albanians elsewhere employed, but in my village, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any reservists who wore green uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were. I did see some on the street. I did not have any problems with them. I just saw them on the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What formations or units did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Nebojsa Nikolic, was that one of your co-villagers? And you said for him that he used to wear a green uniform.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, he was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was a green camouflage uniform you said?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't think I said "Bosko," that Bosko had a green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, I said "Nebojsa Nikolic," and that he wore a green camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Well, they had all kinds of uniforms. You could not tell whether it was police or paramilitary or what kind of clothes they wore. They always would change their clothes. They also had reservist uniforms, army reservist uniforms. Because they had their power in their hands, so they did whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree on one thing, that you don't know what structures or formations Nebojsa Nikolic was part of?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Nebojsa Nikolic sometimes used to wear paramilitary clothes and sometimes police clothes, and I couldn't know what he was, where he belonged, because I did not have any contact with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, can you tell me where he mentioned Nebojsa Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that is in his statement from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I don't have the statement. Where in the evidence has he said anything about that person until you raised him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't mention his statement, but we are talking about the uniforms and his knowledge regarding the uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. But the question you've just asked is: Can we agree on one thing, that you don't know what structure or formations he was part of? Now, where has he suggested he did? You seem to be fighting a statement that's not part of the case at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right, Your Honour. I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And please correct me if I'm wrong --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to be part of the case so far. Am I missing it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are not, but I tried to put it in a wider context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You spoke today about the incident when the women were ordered to go to the lake close to the Albanian border. Who did the policeman address directly when he said that the women were to go towards the lake?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I didn't mention Vermica. I said the police told the women: Stop, and then they divided men from women. Those policemen who we didn't know told us the women: Either go drown yourself in the Drini bar or go to Albania and they took the direction of Drini. I didn't mention Vermica anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This will probably be my mistake. What language did this person use?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: He used the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he also wore a black uniform. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, the black police uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The policeman who ordered you to kneel and to put your hands at the back of your head, did you know him?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No. He was not known to us. I think I mentioned that, that those policemen were not known to us, those who ordered us to keep our hands behind our backs and kneel down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I suppose he also wore a black uniform?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were in the house -- actually in the barn, how were you placed inside? Did they order you to face the wall? How did they tell you to stand when you were in the cowshed?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: They didn't tell us to face the wall, but just move in as we were. Some were standing, some were sitting down on the hay. And then we started to talk a little among ourselves because some elderly men thought that maybe they would maltreat us for a while and then force us to leave to Albania. It never entered our minds that this was going to happen to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would now move on to something else. I would kindly ask you to focus on the trial and your testimony in the late Milosevic case. Mr. Milosevic asked you about the negotiations between the Serbs and the Albanians and their agreement to protect each other from the other side's armed forces. [In English] "-- I wasn't present. Ismail Arifi made the agreement with the Serbs but they didn't keep the agreement. Those that made it did not keep it. The criminals of Krusha e Vogel who shot, burned -- burned 112 people." [Interpretation] This was your response to Mr. Milosevic's question. Did you mean to say that the locals from Krusevo were responsible for the killing of these 112 people, people from Krusha e Vogel?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, they were the organisers or they were participants in what was staged, those who were the ones who led what happened because the people who came from other places didn't know -- the police who came from other places didn't know which houses belonged to Albanians and which not, because it was local Serbs that led them. And they -- I'm not very well-informed of this agreement, but even an agreement was reached; the Serbs didn't abide by it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After that Milosevic asked you whether the Serbs by the name of Petkovic, Vuci Nikolic, Zivcha [phoen], who you've mentioned at the time in your statement, whether they were local guards or local police. Your answer to that was as follows: [In English] "I don't know how they were organised. Sometimes they were there, sometimes they were not. We didn't know who was a policeman and who was not. They all had uniforms."

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could I have a page reference from my learned colleague for that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it's page 6709, line 10 and further on. And we'll offer this transcript at the end as an exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it true, Mr. Ramadani, as you have confirmed it to us partly today, that you didn't know how the local Serbs wearing uniforms were organised.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I was not one of them, but you mentioned Zivchi and Petkovic Vuci. I didn't say they were in uniforms, but I said they were there when the agreement was made with Ismail Arifi. Vuci and Zivchi and Miloshi [phoen], they were the ones who reached the agreement to protect the Albanians against Serbian police or army, and the other side, to protect the Serbs against the KLA. I heard of it. I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us go back and let me ask you where -- this. You didn't know who the uniformed Serbs carrying arms belonged to, what formations they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I don't know that. I told you, they kept changing their uniforms all the time, every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6712, line 19 and onwards Milosevic asked you this: "How many policemen were there in the courtyard next to the cowsheds?"

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I couldn't count them. I saw five or six policemen close by who were standing on guard, but there were other police further away. I was inside. I couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, in the Milosevic trial you mentioned the policemen from the village who were there, the Serb policemen. Were there local policemen, the village policemen, in the vicinity near that place?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I didn't say that there were Serb policemen from the village in fact there; I said that there were policemen. I didn't specify that they were local police. I just said that the police guarded us until other policemen came.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me read you back your answer in English. [In English] "Police of the village, they were Serbs." [Interpretation] This is what you said. Do you remember that you said this?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: But there were local Serb policemen. I say this now and I say this then, but in the place where they were guarding us, I didn't see the local policemen. I remember the local policemen accompanied us when we were taken to the cowshed, but I didn't see them in the cowshed. They were unknown policemen. Maybe the local ones were further away.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Moeller.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think this quote was taken out of the context. There is a sentence before this sentence which should also be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is the preceding sentence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The preceding sentence says: "There were about ten police who guarded us outside and then there came the villagers there, police of the village, they were Serbs." So it refers to both villagers and police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I understand this as: This police refers actually to these police who were outside. And then but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we -- the position's been fully explained now, and we will make what we can of it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramadani, on page 6713, starting with line 24 onwards, you spoke about those who torched the bodies of the men who had been executed. And you say this: [In English] "I was among the dead people and then I went out. I was on the right part where the Serbs of the Krusha e Vogel were there. They were setting fire to the people." [Interpretation] Do you remember and is this correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I didn't say that the Serbs from Krusha e Vogel torched them. When they fired, they entered. Then one who had a pistol shot at anyone who raised the head. I only heard the shots and I saw fire spreading all over us, but I don't know whether it was the local Serbs or the others who did that. The main thing is that this, what I'm saying, happened; that is the execution of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, what was recorded at the Milosevic trial is not correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: It is correct that they burned them, but inside it was impossible for me to see whether the policemen were from the village or were from other places. It was flames all over. Only when I left the place, I saw them in the street, standing in the street. But I didn't have time to look carefully at each and every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I would like to object one more time. It was again taken out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read the context to us, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The context is: "I was inside. I was among the dead people, and then I went out. I was on the right part where the Serbs of Krusha e Vogel were. Then I observed that there were no people on the left part and it was possible for me to leave." The witness has testified today that he saw different people when he came out of the stable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what about the part that says: "They were setting fire to the people"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Yes, that's the part that my learned colleague referred to. Sorry, I left that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will take account of the whole context in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We accept this and we think that this further explains exactly what we want to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ramadani, on page 6719 -- I apologise. Yes, I was correct, 6719, line 19, Milosevic asked you this: [In English] "All right. If there are no witnesses concerning these events, does that mean that you are the sole witness of these events?" And your response was: "I am a witness about the fact that they were executed and burnt. The Serbs of Krusha e Vogel did these things with the help of the people from the neighbouring villages." [Interpretation] Is this correct, what you said at the Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question because I am not very sure I understood it right?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, sir, I can. Mr. Milosevic asked you whether you were a witness and the only witness to this crime. And your response was --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not correct. I object to that. The question referred to the removal of the mortal remains; not of the crime of the shooting in the barn but the aftermath. I would insist that the context is put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me check. Give me one second, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: It is at line 13 of page 6719.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not the only witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ramadani, we're dealing with a matter before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, obviously I skipped this part. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's move to a different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the removal of the bodies, you said that the Serbs from Krusha e Vogel had done that with the help of their neighbours, from the neighbouring villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: There were policemen we didn't know. We didn't know where they were from neighbouring village or from another place, but I do know that the local Serbs guided these policemen to commit the crime they did. And I think I mentioned this. And as to the survivors, there are six and we are all alive. And each and every one of us can testify; you can call them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ramadani, let me ask you this: Based on what you have just told us, could you draw a conclusion that Serb villagers wanted to ethnically cleanse the village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The Serbs have, in general, wanted to cleanse not only Krusha e Vogel, but other places, Krusha e Madhe, Celina, and others. Since they drove all the population out of Albania -- out of Kosova and sent it to Albania, it was an ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: However, you did not attend any other conflicts, you were not involved in any of them; you only know what happened in your own village?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm testifying only about my village, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one moment, Your Honour, just to consult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ramadani. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, only if we can put this transcript into evidence, it's 6D87.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, I think it's necessary that we have the parts in context that have been referred to. Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, do you have questions -- or Ms. Zed, do you have questioned?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour, I'll be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ramadani. My name is Nadia Zed and I just have a few very brief questions for you. First off, sir, I'm just looking at the statement you gave on October 5th, 2001, and it says here that: "In the village there was no regular VJ." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. There was -- the army was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: If we could just look at 4D27 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, the problem, though, Ms. Zed, is that the evidence that the witness has given about the 25th of March is not consistent, and that's what he's thinking about, I'm sure, when he answers your question. Now, are you saying that the statement, which I haven't seen, is actually talking about the 25th of March when that was said?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: The statement actually doesn't give a specific date as to when that observation is made, and I can just read it. It says: "I have been asked if the MUP -- if there were MUP or VJ." And then the part that I quote: "The regular VJ." It goes along a little bit and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, why don't you formulate the question you want to ask, and if you think the answer is inconsistent with the statement, then let's get into the statement, as required.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that on -- on March 25th, 1999, there were a number of different people wearing different uniforms. However, specifically within your -- within your village, there was no regular VJ?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: The tanks and the Pragas were not driven by me. It was not me in them; it was the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, just -- maybe I wasn't clear. I'm not talking about outside your village on -- on the asphalt road; I'm talking about specifically within your village. Does that clarify matters?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Could counsel, before the witness answers, clarify what she means by "regular VJ" to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, she didn't use the word "regular," and therefore I think --

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: I think she did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: The regular army, regular forces, the VJ forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, well, on you go, please ask the question then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sorry, I can just repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just -- just to clarify the question that I've asked. What I'm wondering is if the regular army, the VJ, actually were in your village or outside your village.

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Inside the village, on the streets, I did not see any army. The main road from Prizren-Gjakova, the army was there. And there was army around the village and in the mountains. There were tanks and Pragas. Inside the village there were only policemen -- at least I did not see soldiers inside the village. I think it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: And if we could just take a look at Exhibit P99, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sir, was this how your village looked like in the summer of 1999?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I apologise. This must have been taken later because on the 26th of March there was no vegetation, so these trees here had no leaves. So that's why I think the picture has been taken later.

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me. We investigated in the meantime when this picture was taken because Defence counsel requested us earlier to do so, and we could actually provide the date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what is the date?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: The date is 8 August 2001.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you content with that, Ms. Zed?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Just a final question, Mr. Ramadani. You mentioned a couple of times throughout the day that the people that you saw in your village were at -- on March 25th and thereabouts were changing their uniforms all the time, every day. And, sir, what I'm wondering is: Were these people local Serbs who were putting on different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MS. MOELLER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to object again, but I recall the witness testifying that they could change their uniforms any time they wanted. I don't recall him testifying that they -- that he actually saw them doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm happy that the question is in order. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Sir, can you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: I apologise, but it's not clear to me. Could you repeat it?

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Certainly, certainly. You've mentioned a couple of times today that the people that you saw in your village on and around the -- March 25th, 1999, were changing their uniforms all the time, every day. And, sir, what I'm wondering is whether these people were local Serbs who were putting on different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: LUTFI RAMADANI
utterances.text: Yes, locals, locals.

utterances.speaker: MS. ZED
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those are all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. O'Sullivan, do you have questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will probably need some ten minutes or so, and I understand that my colleague, Visnjic, also has questions, so I don't know whether we are going to continue today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm going to have half an hour, and we are running rather late. We have a meeting at 5.30, so I would really very much appreciate it if we could adjourn and if I could continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Mr. Ramadani, we have to bring the proceedings for today to an end now, which means you will have to come back and continue your evidence tomorrow, and that will be at 9.00 tomorrow. Between now and then, it is absolutely vital that you do not discuss any part of your evidence with any person at all, and that means either the evidence you've given or the evidence that you may yet give in the court. You can talk about anything else you wish, with anyone you wish, but please do not discuss the evidence. Now, if you sit there for a moment until we leave the court, then -- in fact, no, it would be better if you go with the usher now and he'll show you where to go and we'll see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall resume at 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
